About twenty percent of these are children under the age of five. In the past two years, eight people have died of complications related to measles. That is more deaths than in the thirty years before that combined. Deaths In February 2025, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. was appointed Minister of Health in the Trump <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> administration. For years he was one of the loudest vaccine critics in the US. For example, shortly after taking office he dismissed all the experts on the vaccine advisory committee and partly replaced them with vaccine sceptics. After several deaths from measles, he somewhat softened his positions on the disease. For instance, he stated that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent the spread of the disease. But the consequences of his criticism are already becoming visible. The vaccination rate is now already below the 95 percent needed to contain the spread of measles. As a result, infection figures are rising rapidly in several states. In November, international health officials will meet to determine whether the US and Mexico have lost their status as measles-free countries. A country must go twelve months without cases of the disease to be declared measles-free. Disinformation about vaccines and problems with access to healthcare also cause some parents not to have themselves or their children vaccinated. Salmonella Alongside measles outbreaks, the US is also struggling with a number of foodborne diseases. For example, this year nearly 13,000 Americans developed diarrhoea and other stomach and abdominal complaints from eating lettuce contaminated with the intestinal parasite. The American Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has since traced the contamination to a Mexican farm. American media report that food products in the US are increasingly being recalled due to contamination by bacteria, viruses or parasites. This concerns eggs, chicken or meat, among other things. According to various media, this development is caused by budget cuts and staff leaving the FDA and the US Department of Agriculture, which puts food inspections under pressure. The American health service CDC is currently investigating 33 outbreaks of food-related diseases, including salmonella, E. coli and listeria.

title: Drone attack on ships off Bulgarian coast, prime minister holds emergency meeting
lead: A ship has sunk off the coast of Bulgaria in the Black Sea after a drone attack. A fire broke out on another ship, Bulgarian President Iotova confirms in a statement. According to Prime Minister Radev, the crew of the sunken ship is missing. It is not clear how many people are involved. A search operation has been launched for them. Eighteen crew members have been rescued from the burning ship. Some have been taken to hospital in Varna, on Bulgaria's east coast. Local media report that one of them has serious burns, and another is reportedly injured in the head. Several others have minor injuries. Cargo ships. According to media sources, these are cargo ships. The sunken ship, named Alfa Watan, sailed under the flag of Togo. It is not known what cargo the ship was carrying. The ship where the fire broke out, named Able, sailed under the flag of Palau. That ship is known to have been carrying grain. The attack took place at around 03.00 local time, about 112 kilometres from the coast, still within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. That country is a member of NATO. After the incident, both ships sent out distress signals. Bulgarian Prime Minister Radev held an emergency meeting with the relevant ministries and security services. It is not yet clear whether this was an attack with drones in the air, sea drones, or both. Reference to war between Russia and Ukraine. It is not yet clear who is behind the drone attack. However, in a televised statement, the Bulgarian prime minister referred to the Russian war in Ukraine. Reuters news agency, citing a source in maritime security, writes that initial analyses of the attack point to it likely being a Russian attack. "If this war does not end in time, the risk of a global conflict grows," said Prime Minister Radev. "We see that the war is escalating: all rules of international law are being violated and civilian ships are being attacked at sea. This is completely unacceptable." Russia has not yet responded to the incident. Fire on Turkish ship. The attack follows shortly after a fire on a ship in the Black Sea yesterday, outside the territorial waters of Romania. Two people died in that incident, and eleven crew members could be rescued. The Romanian Ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> says it is not yet known what caused that fire. Ukrainian President Zelensky accuses Russia of a drone attack on a Turkish ship carrying maize. Since the start of the war between Ukraine and Russia four years ago, several European countries have had to deal with Russian drones violating their airspace, as well as with mines in the Black Sea on important trade and energy routes.

title: 'Swimming lessons for children with disabilities need to be more accessible'
lead: For children with a disability, swimming lessons are not always a given, especially when their parents have money worries. Municipal income support for these parents falls short, says the Mulier Institute, which carried out research on the subject. Swimming lessons for children with a disability are often more expensive than regular swimming lessons. The research shows that children benefit from smaller groups of four or two pupils and sometimes even one-on-one lessons. "That is so they have fewer distractions from other children and get more attention from their teacher," explains researcher Mirjam Stuij of the Mulier Institute. A swimming instructor also needs to know how to handle a child with a disability. These two factors make adapted swimming lessons more expensive. "That is difficult for parents, but also for swimming instructors." Existing schemes fall short Municipalities already offer schemes and allowances, but these are sometimes unclear and differ from municipality to municipality. Parents run into several issues when applying, Stuij explains. "For example, the allowance they receive does not cover the cost of the swimming lessons." There are also parents who formally have too high an income, but who, because of high care costs or other high costs due to the child's disability, still have money worries. They therefore do not qualify. Thirdly, the institute sees that applying for schemes can demand a lot from parents. This is because information from the municipality is unclear or because parents do not know where to turn. Fewer or no certificates Stuij stresses that parents consider a swimming certificate of great importance. "If my child falls into a ditch, I want them to be able to save themselves. I think we can all picture that very well in the Netherlands." Figures from the <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-bureau-voor-de-statistiek">CBS</entity> show that 14 percent of children living in poverty have a disability, compared with 8 percent of children not living in poverty. Figures from Mulier also show that children with a disability obtain a swimming certificate at a later age, fewer certificates, or no swimming certificate at all. Clarity and flexibility The institute advises municipalities to map out how things are arranged for them, what the municipality reimburses and for whom. "Because we know that varies enormously," says Stuij. The research leads to a number of recommendations for local governments. For example, good information provision for parents should be established and the application process should be made as clear as possible. The institute calls for more flexibility in income support. For example, a standard allowance that can be increased if the costs for a child are higher, Stuij explains. The institute also advises appointing a fixed point of contact for parents. "Someone who can help them with the application and, for example, with finding suitable swimming lessons."

title: Event organisers in Breda send urgent letter about higher permit costs
lead: Eighteen event organisations in Breda, such as Breda Jazz, Ploegendienst and carnival activities, have together sent an urgent letter to the city council. They demand more transparency about the announced price increases for event permits, writes Omroep Brabant . From 2027 the municipality will increase the costs of an event permit. For example, the cost of a permit for large events, such as the big carnival parade, will rise from 17.000 euro to nearly 37.000 euro. For smaller events, the rate will double from 4900 to just over 10.000 euro. 'It is not going to work' The organisations fear that the higher costs will be the downfall of some events. Stichting Kielegat, a volunteer organisation for carnival activities in the city, says it cannot afford the price increase. "I see no possibility of raising that amount extra within a year. It is simply not going to work", said chairman Rutger Westenburg after the announcement. The Breda Jazz Festival attracts around 250.000 visitors each year. Even so, the price increase also shocked chairwoman Hanneke Griffioen. "It is a substantial amount, so you blink and then think: am I reading this correctly?" She therefore wants to sit down with the municipality. "Because this is not a normal price increase." The municipality says the higher costs are necessary because for many years Breda has only passed on around twenty percent of the costs related to permit applications. "We have tried to keep the increase limited, but unfortunately... Everything is getting more expensive", said the responsible alderman Arjen van Drunen. According to Van Drunen, even after the increase the full costs are still not covered. Transparency Among the signatories of the letter are volunteer organisations, but also commercial organisers. Koninklijke Horeca Nederland Breda and organised hospitality entrepreneurs have also joined. "We above all want transparency with all these organisations about how these permit fees have been built up", says Johan de Vos of Koninklijke Horeca Nederland Breda. "We want to see what the justification is. That this is a broadly supported demand is clear from all the organisations that have backed this letter." The organisers demand access to the full calculation behind the new rates. They want to know how many official hours are charged, which hourly rates are passed on, and whether costs for enforcement, public order and traffic measures have been included in the rates. Afterwards they want to discuss with the municipality which part of the costs organisers should pay. According to them, it should be clear which costs really belong to the permit and which belong to the municipality's normal tasks. "The mere fact that certain work takes place around events does not automatically mean that these costs can be recovered from the individual organiser through event fees", they write. The event organisations also want to examine whether the permit process can be made cheaper.

title: Heavy art book with work by Dalí stolen from French museum
lead: One of the most expensive and heaviest books in the world has been stolen from a museum in France. The cover of the artwork Apocalypse, made by Salvador Dalí alone, weighs 150 kilos. It is a mystery how the thieves got the extremely heavy book out of the building. The public prosecutor has started an investigation into the theft in the municipality of Issoire, about a hundred kilometres west of Lyon. The police have not released details about the art theft in the night from Sunday to Monday. It is unclear whether there are suspects. 'Murder of heritage' The owner of the artwork calls the theft an attack on the French cultural sector. "France has been murdered last night. French heritage has been murdered", Christian Karoutzos said yesterday evening to French media. The Apocalypse was made between 1958 and 1961 and weighs about 210 kilos in total. Fourteen of the most renowned artists of that time contributed to the project. The famous Spanish painter Dalí made the bronze cover. Dalí was one of the best-known artists of the last century. He painted surrealist works and was an eccentric person. He wore a distinctive thin moustache, with the tips curled upwards. The moustache is "the most serious part of my personality", Dalí once said jokingly in an interview.

title: Cat-theft ring in Vietnam busted: 'Thousands of animals stolen'
lead: The Vietnamese <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has dismantled a network responsible for the theft of thousands of cats in Ho Chi Minh City. Twelve men are suspected of stealing and reselling the animals, presumably for consumption, state media report. The main suspect is 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh, who is the suspected gang leader. According to the police investigation, Binh bought live cats and stored them at a location in the city before reselling them. Several people worked under him, who in turn recruited others to steal cats in different parts of the city. The network consisted of small groups, each with its own area. At night, the groups went through residential neighbourhoods on motorbikes in search of cats. They made their own cat traps. According to the suspects, each group stole four to ten cats per night. 50 cats rescued In July, the police raided the Dong Thanh district. 50 cats were rescued during the raid. Dozens of cat traps, scales, mobile phones, motorbikes, clippers and cash were also seized. Of the 50 rescued cats, thirteen have since been reunited with their owners, while the search for the other owners continues. During questioning, the suspects reportedly admitted to having stolen a total of 2,700 cats. It is not known exactly how long the gang was active. During an earlier raid in June, 400 cats were rescued. The animals were locked up in 45 cages. During that raid, more than 80 dead cats were also found, which were being kept cold with ice. Nine people were arrested. Eating cats and dogs Eating cats and dogs is not illegal in Vietnam, provided sellers hold the proper licences. The police emphasise that knowingly buying illegal meat is punishable, as is trading in stolen animals. There are no official figures on the local consumption of dogs and cats, but resistance to it has been growing in Vietnam in recent years. Particularly among young people and pet owners, writes animal welfare organisation Humane World for Animals. They point to the cruelty and animal abuse involved in the illegal catching, trade, storage and transport of the animals. But there is also increasing opposition because cats and dogs are increasingly seen as companion animals and not as food.

title: Online trade in 'blackmail packages' of women, Belgium and Netherlands investigate
lead: <entity id="person:david-van-weel">Minister Van Weel</entity> (VVD) of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity> will ask the Dutch <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> to offer help to the Belgian police, who are investigating the trade in nude photos of women on the so-called darkweb. He said this in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>, where he was asked questions about the case, which RTL reported. Nude photos and private data of hundreds of Belgian and Dutch women are being traded on the hidden part of the internet, RTL reported. Ready-made packages with intimate photos, social media profiles and contact details are offered on a site that has been active since 2023. Women can be harassed and blackmailed with them. For one euro per victim, access to private data and photos is provided. The 'packages' are sold to several people at once. The website offers, for a payment of 250 euros, to remove the data from the platform, but it is unclear whether this actually happens. 'Perverse practices' There is great revulsion across the House. Minister Van Weel spoke of appalling practices of a "perversity you do not often see". He also expressed his sympathy with the victims. One of the victims is a 31-year-old woman from Limburg who told her story to RTL. She had panic attacks when she heard she was on the site. Fifteen years later her photos still keep appearing. Van Weel called her story shocking and believes she is doing fantastic work, including by removing the shame felt by victims. MPs want justice to act firmly, if necessary at European level. "This concerns organised sexual violence", says VVD MP Becker. "These are not incidents, but a business model", says Pro MP Mutluer. The House wants the site to go offline as soon as possible. Parties also want the Dutch <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> to be involved in the case quickly. 'Investigation difficult' What is happening here is punishable, but investigating it will not be easy, says Van Weel. "It is technically not simple to find out who is behind it on the darkweb, where the server is, how a site can go offline". Van Weel says he "cannot take the darkweb offline with a bill tomorrow". According to him there are ways to take sites offline, but "first very specific technical investigations are needed, and we will certainly commit to those". The Belgian police have announced an investigation and Van Weel will ask the Dutch police to "consult the Antwerp police and see how we can help". The Dutch Openbaar Ministerie is not yet conducting an investigation into the case, a spokesperson told the NOS, but the OM does not rule out joining a later international joint investigation. "Given the facts and the number of potential Dutch victims, it would make sense if a request for help comes from Belgium; then we are also willing to help." Can you check whether your data has been leaked? For anyone worried after this news about whether her data or photos can be found on the darkweb, there is unfortunately no satisfactory answer: there is currently no simple way to search for that, says a spokesperson for the knowledge centre Offlimits to the NOS. "We do not advise people to search the darkweb themselves for their name or images. As far as we know there is no public and safe way to check that yourself on the darkweb." Moreover, she warns: "You don't know what you will encounter there. Other illegal or very shocking material can also be found in such environments. You also have no control over what appears on a page. Moreover, searching yourself gives no certainty whether you are or are not on the website. If you don't find your name, that does not automatically mean you are not in the database. And conversely, a namesake can of course cause confusion. It may also disrupt a police investigation." Her tip is: "Do you have concerns or concrete indications that your images or data have been shared, for example because someone is contacting or threatening you with them? Then get in touch with Offlimits or the police. We can look together at what is going on and which steps you can take."

title: Adults predominantly positive about LGBTI people, well-being of some groups 'concerning'
lead: Broadly speaking, the views of adult Dutch people on, for example, homosexuality are unchanged compared with two years ago. There are, however, large differences between the individual LGBTI+ groups. Moreover, the well-being of the groups varies greatly. This emerges from the biennial Lhbtiqa+monitor by Movisie, Panteia and Ipsos I&O. In September, another study revealed that acceptance of homosexuality among young people has declined over the past four years. That study was conducted among young people between the ages of 12 and 16. Who is this study about? The Lhbtiqa+monitor is a study carried out every two years on behalf of <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>. The abbreviation stands for the groups the study is about: lesbian, homosexual, bisexual, transgender, intersex, queer, asexual and non-binary persons. Not only their living situation is addressed. Every two years the researchers also ask about Dutch people's views on these groups. Although homosexuality is still predominantly viewed positively (84 percent), a slight shift is visible. Compared with two years ago, slightly more respondents think 'neutrally' about this group instead of 'positively'. The share of respondents who judge homosexuality negatively has remained stable (4 percent). Views on other groups have also remained broadly the same when compared with two years ago. The fact that little has changed in general is considered concerning by researcher Karijn van den Berg of Movisie. "Views on, for example, homosexuality are generally positive, but that applies much less to intersex, transgender and non-binary persons," the researcher said. When you zoom in on groups, changes are indeed visible. For instance, 65 percent of those surveyed found sex between two men "not disgusting" in 2024, while that number has now fallen to 60 percent. Moreover, more than a quarter of respondents have "difficulty with" kissing in public, mainly when it concerns two men. Two years ago that applied to about a fifth of Dutch people. Gender or sexual identity as a 'fashion phenomenon' The study also shows that being transgender, non-binary and bisexual is relatively often seen as a fashion phenomenon by those surveyed. That concerns the researchers. They also find it concerning that many respondents do not want a relationship with transgender, non-binary, bisexual, asexual or intersex persons. Another conclusion of the researchers is the limited knowledge about asexual, non-binary and intersex persons. Many questions about these groups are not answered by the respondents. They often indicate not knowing the answer or never having thought about it. "This finding shows that the knowledge about and understanding, or recognition, of these groups of persons in Dutch society is still fairly limited," the report states. The researchers did not only look at Dutch people's views on the individual LGBTI+ groups. They also mapped the well-being of those groups themselves. There too the differences between the groups are large, the report shows. Well-being of LGBTI+ persons Where the living situation of homosexual persons is generally comparable to that of heterosexuals, that of intersex, transgender and non-binary persons can be called concerning, the report states. For instance, they more often deal with depression, suicidal thoughts, financial problems and discrimination, a survey among these groups shows. Researcher Van den Berg calls these large differences in well-being between the studied groups "very striking". "We see a real gap between, for example, homosexual and transgender people, both in terms of acceptance and in terms of well-being." The researchers make a number of recommendations to the cabinet. For instance, they advise education and information about sexual and gender diversity. They also recommend paying attention to online hate and disinformation about LGBTI+ persons in lessons about media literacy. Attention to the studied groups in vocational training programmes in care and welfare and more room for inclusive policy in government are other recommendations. The groups the study is about Lesbian persons: women who are attracted to women. Homosexual persons: men who are attracted to men. Bi+ persons: persons who are attracted to more than one gender. Transgender persons: people whose gender identity does not (fully) correspond with the sex assigned at birth. Non-binary persons: people who identify as non-binary, feel at home with a gender identity outside the (binary) categories of man and woman. Intersex persons: are born with a body that does not correspond with the image most people have of man or woman. Queer persons: people who cannot find themselves in the usual, fixed (binary) frameworks and boxes for gender and/or sexual orientation, or reject these frameworks. Asexual persons: people who experience no or little sexual attraction to other persons.

title: IND must work through 140,000 Ukrainian applications, asylum system under further pressure
lead: The asylum applications of over 140,000 Ukrainians that have been put on the shelf must still be reviewed and assessed. This follows from a ruling of the European Court of Justice. Among administrators it is beginning to filter through that this could have major consequences for the pressure on the asylum chain, according to those involved. <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> also admits that it has a problem. Ukrainians who came to the Netherlands because of the war fell under the Temporary Protection Directive. This EU-devised rule allows displaced persons to receive temporary protection. The Netherlands arranged it so that if you wanted that protection, you also had to submit an asylum application. That application was then automatically suspended. And parking asylum applications is not allowed, the European court ruled last week. "We have long chosen not to handle applications from Ukrainians in the Netherlands, because they already received protection," says responsible minister Van den Brink of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-am">Asiel en Migratie</entity>. "Also because it was a very large number. The court now clearly says: it must be done," the minister said. Extra pressure on the asylum chain. Asylum lawyer Wil Eikelboom: "In hindsight it was not such a good idea to link temporary protection to submitting an asylum application. Quite awkward." In other countries no asylum application was automatically filed when someone fell under the Temporary Protection Directive. "The Netherlands really is an exception there," says Ricky van Oers, university lecturer in Sociology of Law and Migration Law at Radboud University. All applications from Ukrainians must therefore now be handled. "The question is how the IND is going to do this, they actually have no capacity for it at all," says Eikelboom. The minister admits that this ruling of the court will "certainly add extra pressure" to the asylum system. "At the same time the court also offers room," the minister states, hoping this way to make his problem manageable. He interprets the ruling so that he does not have to handle the applications of all Ukrainians immediately. Van den Brink first wants to handle the asylum applications of people who are arriving now, and at the same time the more than fifty thousand people who were already on the waiting list, and only then give priority to this group of Ukrainians. In short: yes, the asylum applications of the Ukrainians must be handled, but the minister wants to wait with most of them for now. According to university lecturer in migration law Van Oers there are indeed nuances to the ruling of the European Court. "Because it concerns so many applications, the Netherlands may be able to handle the procedures in phases. They can also decide to give priority to certain groups, for example families." But the question is how much room the minister's approach will actually provide, because all of this will certainly mean extra work. 'Permanent temporariness' The advantage of that directive for Ukrainians was, for example, that they could work here immediately, unlike asylum seekers. It also temporarily grants the right to shelter, medical care and education for children. But that also brings uncertainty. "Ukrainians live here in permanent temporariness," says Van Oers. "Because of that temporary protection there is continually little prospect of building a life. While in fact there is an asylum application pending. Such an asylum status gives more certainty." The temporary protection of Ukrainians runs until March 2028. It is still unclear whether it will be extended afterwards. According to Vluchtelingenwerk the ruling of the European Court of Justice has probably not yet reached many Ukrainians. "But it undoubtedly leads to more unrest and uncertainty. Return to Ukraine is currently not a realistic option." Vluchtelingenwerk wants a sustainable plan for Ukrainians in the Netherlands. "With a fast and careful assessment of their residence permits, so that these people, who have already experienced a great deal, know where they stand." The highest administrative judge in the Netherlands must now assess the European ruling. Afterwards it will become clear what its significance is in practice. According to lawyers, the Netherlands cannot simply ignore the ruling in any case.

title: Podcast De Dag: what makes the French schoolchildren's protests ever bigger
lead: The French secondary school protest is growing, more violent and more political. Today, during a national protest day, certainly tens of thousands, according to the union even hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets in solidarity with French students. The protest erupted two weeks ago, at the start of the school year. It concerns a shortage of teachers, deficient timetables and materials. And inequality: schools in the banlieues are hit much harder than schools elsewhere. Listening? You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. In the podcast De Dag, Dutch students Raoul and Felix, who study in France, tell what they see happening around them and what moves their fellow students. Niek Pas is a France expert at the UvA and also previously taught in France. According to him, we must also view the protests in light of the upcoming presidential elections. Politicians are jumping on the unrest and pointing fingers at each other about the causes of the poor state of education. Respond? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation and editing: Elisabeth Steinz Editorial: Max Smedes and Wouter Sloekers Final editing: Judith van de Hulsbeek

title: Free ice cream action gets out of hand, police step in
lead: An action in which an ice cream parlour handed out free ice creams in Almere got out of hand yesterday. The many young people present became so unruly that, on police advice, the shop had to close its doors. "We wanted to do something good for the neighbourhood and this is what we get," the owner told Omroep Flevoland . The free ice cream action reached many young people. On TikTok the announcement was viewed more than 130,000 times. According to the entrepreneur, the first hour went without problems, but the atmosphere changed after that. Sent away According to the owner there was pushing and pulling, and young people harassed staff. "We almost had to work as bodyguards instead of as ordinary staff." Eventually the police were called. According to the entrepreneur, several vehicles arrived on the scene and officers went into the shop with a police dog. A police spokesperson says the young people were sent away but that no one was arrested. The owner is disappointed. "We wanted to bring people together and organise something fun. But of course our staff need to be able to work safely."

title: French prime minister: no lessons at French schools in the coming days, talking with each other
lead: There will be no lessons at all lycées throughout France for the next three days. That is what French prime minister Lecornu has said. The reason is the large-scale school student protests of the past weeks. Lycées are the upper secondary schools, for students from about 15 years of age. The prime minister wants, together with the minister of Education, to give a political answer to the protests. He hopes that schools and students will enter into dialogue with each other in the coming days. It is not clear whether schools will respond to this or whether schools want to keep lessons going. Lecornu calls the protests "real" and believes that students must be listened to. He also named a number of points of attention on which the government can work, such as the state of the school buildings. Protests today too. Today too tens of thousands of people took to the streets in French cities. It was the largest day of action since the protests began last month. Hundreds of schools were closed again. In the meantime, trade unions and parents have also rallied behind the protests. According to the ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, at least 250,000 people are out today. One of the trade unions speaks of 450,000 demonstrators, even before the large demonstration in Paris began. Tens of thousands of people are also expected there during a march. In several places along the route the mood is grim. Pupils and students demand more money for education. They are furious about the poor state of the school buildings and the teacher shortage. In several cities the police used tear gas. In Strasbourg, Lyon and Rennes among others, demonstrators set fires and threw objects at the police. According to prime minister Lecornu, 85 teachers and 215 pupils were injured in the protests of the past days. He calls it "the heaviest toll that education staff has suffered in decades". 715 police officers were also injured in the protests.

title: Once again large protests and violence in France, what is behind it?
lead: It has been unrest in France for a few weeks now. What began as a small-scale protest at a secondary school outside Paris has grown into a national popular movement, which university students have also joined. At the same time, hooligans or rioters are abusing the demonstrations. Where does this unrest come from? Whereas in recent days it was still about hundreds of schools, demonstrators today blocked 1800 secondary schools. According to the ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, at least 250,000 people took to the streets, from Rennes and Toulouse to Paris, to further increase pressure on the French government. Education and teachers' unions are also taking part. The demonstrators want an end to a series of problems in French education, such as the poor condition of school buildings. The police are cracking down hard: last week 5000 people were arrested, 87 percent of whom were minors. On 17 September, pupils in a suburb of Paris decided to block the entrance to their secondary school. They wanted to take a stand against overcrowded classes and long school days. The pupils were not alone; they received support from teachers who voiced their concerns about the shortage of staff and materials, and the high workload. French secondary school pupils are required to have more lesson hours than their peers in many other European countries. "I leave home at half past six in the morning and when I get back it's seven in the evening. I see my teachers more often than my family. That is not normal", says a pupil from Val-de-Marne to local media. Vulnerable neighbourhoods In addition, many French secondary schools struggle with a shortage of basic facilities such as tables and chairs. Due to a lack of air conditioning, temperatures in classrooms rise sharply during heatwaves, while in winter it can be bitterly cold. Pupils point to deferred maintenance, which leads to leaking roofs, cockroaches and rat infestations, as in Saint-Denis. According to activists, these problems are often most severe at schools in socioeconomically vulnerable neighbourhoods. Parcoursup, the platform through which pupils apply for further education, is also under fire. Sometimes pupils have to wait months until they know whether they will be admitted to their chosen course of study. According to many of them, the system causes uncertainty and extra stress about their future. Police violence The first demonstration was still fairly peaceful, with a few rubbish bins set on fire. But images spread rapidly via social media and protests spread to other cities outside Paris. The movement received almost immediate support from the radical left party La France Insoumise (LFI), which has a strong following among young people. That support is electorally significant, as some of the pupils will be allowed to vote in the French presidential election for the first time next year. Right-wing politicians accuse the party of fuelling and politicising the protest. For example, the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, said that violence "is legitimate in some cases". These words, which according to Bagayoko were taken out of context, caused much uproar. Centre-right presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau asked whether LFI should not be banned. LFI leader Mélenchon, on the other hand, argues that his party only supports the movement and does not organise it. He wants the demonstrations to remain non-violent and points to what he describes as the police's "brutality". According to him, officers frequently used tear gas and batons to disperse demonstrators. Yesterday, in the French city of Lens, a 15-year-old pupil lost his hand after picking up a stun grenade that had been thrown by riot police. Nearly 200 pupils and teachers have since been injured. Despite the disorder, the demonstrators are continuing. So today at least 250,000 people took to the streets. According to one of the unions, there were even 450,000. On Sunday, Prime Minister Lecornu wrote a letter in which he promises to come up with concrete commitments for pupils this week, including making school buildings better able to withstand the effects of climate change. In addition, 1,2 billion euros extra is being allocated to education in the budget, which still has to be approved by parliament. He also announced that no lessons will be given at secondary schools up to and including Friday, in the hope that schools and pupils will then enter into dialogue with each other. But the fear is that the genie is already out of the bottle and that the protest movement could grow into a much broader popular movement. This is also because there is a lot of frustration in France about high fuel prices. The Yellow Vests movement, which largely paralysed France in 2018, has announced it will return to the streets on 17 October.

title: Dispute over box 3: coalition divided over paper gifts
lead: The coalition is once again internally divided over how the changes to the wealth tax (box 3) should be paid for. <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> wants to tax wealthy people differently from 2028 and wants to introduce a so-called capital gains tax on savings, investments and a second home (box 3). A tax that is no longer levied annually on the growth of your wealth, but only afterwards, for example once you have sold shares. Parties think this is fairer for the wealthy. But the change to the system will create a gap of billions in the budget in the coming years. D66 and CDA agree, with a majority in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Kamer</entity>, that part of the gap can be closed by tackling the 'paper gift tax'. That is a tax-advantaged way to give money and thereby pay less inheritance tax. But the VVD does not want that to happen. "We are not going to touch that", says VVD <entity id="person:ruben-pieter-brekelmans">fractievoorzitter Brekelmans</entity> firmly. When asked how things should proceed, he says: "We will see, the cabinet is now going to work on it further." Looking for funding During the General Financial Deliberations last week, great dissatisfaction arose over the way the cabinet wanted to cover the capital gains tax. The plan was to have a group of about 1.5 million investors with assets from 30,000 euros pay tax already next year. In addition, more savers and investors in the new system, which is due to start in 2028, would for the first time pay wealth tax: from a profit above 1,000 euros. Both plans therefore did not go ahead. The cabinet then asked parties to come up with their own funding proposals. Today the ChristenUnie came with the proposal to tackle paper gifts as funding. That can count on a majority in the Kamer, but not on the undivided support of the coalition. 'Bickering is enough' CDA <entity id="person:hendrik-bontenbal">leider Bontenbal</entity> thinks tackling the tax advantage of the paper gift tax is a good plan. That the VVD thinks differently should be possible in a minority coalition, he says. He does not know "what the outcome will be". The ChristenUnie is "fed up with the bickering after all these months". As far as ChristenUnie <entity id="person:mirjam-hannah-bikker">leider Bikker</entity> is concerned, the VVD must now move "from no to together". "You are allowed to have a few sacred cows, but at some point the conversation has to follow." The VVD itself has a different plan to close the gap in box 3: lower the tax rate for entrepreneurs in box 2 even more than the current plans provide. The idea is that entrepreneurs will thereby be enticed to withdraw more money from their business. If more entrepreneurs do so, extra money temporarily flows into the treasury. The plan to go even further than the cabinet already wanted received a majority. In the long term, it is incidentally not enough to cover the transition to box 3. If the cabinet manages to cover box 3, another problem then awaits. A Kamer majority is against raising the income taxes that are to yield 8 billion euros in the coming years. A majority from left to right calls on the cabinet to adjust those plans.

title: Neder-Betuwe threatens 24 rioters with fines if it goes wrong again
lead: <entity id="person:jan-kottelenberg">Burgemeester Kottelenberg</entity> of Neder-Betuwe wants to prevent the rioters involved in the anti-asylum-centre demonstrations in September from causing more trouble. He will therefore fine them at any future demonstration that gets out of hand. It concerns 24 people. In a column on the municipality's website, Kottelenberg rejected the behaviour of those involved. According to the mayor, four officers suffered hearing damage because rioters had thrown heavy fireworks. Demonstrators also smashed the windows of the town hall, insulted the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> and did not follow the officers' orders. To prevent this, the mayor has now decided to impose a so-called order subject to a penalty. The 24 persons may no longer be involved in or present at disturbances during demonstrations anywhere in the municipality of Neder-Betuwe, reports Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-gelderland">Gelderland</entity>. If they do, they will receive a fine of at least 5000 euros and at most 15,000 euros per violation. The penalty applies for an indefinite period. Imposing an order subject to a penalty is regularly used against rioters, but much less often against demonstrators who are merely present at riots. Asked, both the police and a municipal spokesperson could not answer whether the measure conflicts with the right to demonstrate. Not on the agenda: a new demonstration against asylum reception has been announced for Thursday evening at the municipal hall in Opheusden in Neder-Betuwe. A college information evening will take place then. Asylum reception is incidentally not on the agenda for that evening. The municipality expects around a hundred young people to attend the demonstration again. The municipality has already made contact with the organiser of the protests, in the hope of reaching agreements. For example, the municipality wants to designate an area where demonstrators can stand.

title: Espionage case damages reputation of German intelligence service
lead: "An absolute nightmare scenario", says intelligence expert Kenneth Lasoen about the news that the former head of Germany's foreign intelligence service has been arrested. Lasoen is professor of intelligence and security studies at the University of Antwerp. Former BND chief August Hanning (80) was arrested today on suspicion of treason and espionage. Also arrested was his closest associate and confidant Manfred D., who is also chief of staff to Hanning's successor. It is not known for which foreign service Hanning is alleged to have spied. One of the few indications is a remark by a member of the German parliament. In a response to the arrests, that person said that working "for the enemies of liberal democracy" will not be tolerated. "But even then we still have a fairly long list of countries", says professor Lasoen to the NOS. Der Spiegel writes this evening that the investigators assume Hanning was in contact with an agent of Azerbaijan's secret service, but that has not been confirmed. 2000 documents Hanning was head of the BND from 1998 to 2005 and then state secretary of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> until the end of 2009. He then continued as a private security adviser. The German public prosecutor suspects that in spring 2010, so after his time as BND head and state secretary, he agreed with Manfred D. that D. would provide him, for payment, with valuable information from BND files. According to the prosecutor, D. passed nearly 2000 BND documents to Hanning until June 2022, including a large number marked as "secret document" for internal use. In at least one case, Hanning used documents to make an analysis for staff of a foreign security service, according to the prosecutor. What that analysis concerned and whether it ended up with that service is not yet known to the prosecutor. Usual suspects The Süddeutsche Zeitung and the regional public broadcasters NDR and WDR carried out extensive research into the case. They were told that Hanning did not work for Russia. Kenneth Lasoen would not be surprised if it was China. "But it could just as well have been another country. The usual suspects are always Russia and China, but there are other services that use these kinds of techniques." Germany correspondent Chiem Balduk: "Although the full extent is not yet clear, there is rightly talk in Germany of a major scandal. The BND thrives on trust and needs it precisely now. The service wants more powers to better get a grip on espionage and sabotage from Russia. Instead of only gathering information, the organisation must be reformed into a 'real' secret service that can also carry out missions abroad. That still has to be voted on in the Bundestag. This affair has not made that vote easier. You can call for more powers, but mainly this raises the question of whether the service needs more oversight." It is of course a humiliation for a security service when secrets are taken from under its nose and passed to an enemy. "Then the first question is: what information has been compromised?", says Lasoen. "Who has it in hand and what impact has that had on German national security?" On top of that, leaking information endangers cooperation with friendly security services. "It does the BND's reputation with its international partners no good when there is a chance that shared information ends up in the hands of hostile intelligence services. That could well have many consequences." Side finding What makes the case even more painful for the BND is that the suspicions against Hanning and his former chief of staff came to light by chance. The prosecutor's office in Hamburg was investigating the failed abduction of a child in 2022. In that investigation, a security company came into view with which Hanning worked. In September 2025 there was a raid on his home near Münster. Investigators took away crates full of documents. Analysing what all of it contained took months. Only a few months ago was the BND informed of the discovery of the documents. In May of this year, the national public prosecutor took over the case from the colleagues in Hamburg.

title: House hopes to be able to deploy 130,000 citizens in crises
lead: The <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">Tweede Kamer</entity> is taken with the initiative to train citizens to support the emergency services during disasters or crises. A majority today supported a motion from the CDA expressing the wish to have 130,000 of these so-called civilian reservists within four years. In a major crisis, the volunteers must help prevent chaos, especially in the first three days. <entity id="org:politie">Politie</entity>, the army and the emergency services cannot handle the work alone, is the expectation. The reservists must be trained in three specialisms: technology, logistics and security. This involves, for example, mechanics, drivers and security guards. They must form a kind of second layer around the armed forces. The organisation BurgerReserve has already given training in general skills to about a thousand Dutch people this year. The costs are paid by businesses and private individuals. In kind The House now wants <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> to contribute to the expansion to 130,000 civilian reservists. Not with money, but in kind, by making training grounds and classrooms of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-defensie">Defensie</entity> available free of charge. The cabinet has already said it shares the House's wish. What do such training sessions look like? Nieuwsuur visited one: "The way we normally do things will no longer work", says director <entity id="person:karen-van-oudenhoven-van-der-zee">Karen van Oudenhoven-van der Zee</entity> of the <entity id="org:sociaal-en-cultureel-planbureau">Sociaal en Cultureel Planbureau</entity> to Nieuwsuur. Her organisation advocates strengthening the resilience of citizens so that crises can be better absorbed. She names war as a possible crisis, both in the Netherlands and elsewhere. Or the consequences of climate change, such as floods. "It may be that some products suddenly are no longer on supermarket shelves. Or there will be power outages or IT failures, making transport impossible." Catching up After the Second World War, the Netherlands long had the idea that we had a grip on everything that could befall us, says Van Oudenhoven. "The corona crisis was actually the first moment we realised: something can easily happen that makes us lose that grip. There is now more tension in the world than ever since the Second World War. In terms of resilience, we have some catching up to do." As for national threats, the government has so far placed a great deal of emphasis on defence, she says. "What you see is that a lot of attention goes to investment in weapons and the army. And that relatively little attention is paid to people and society. The budget in the Miljoenennota for neighbourhoods is 40 million. That is for 2027. After that it becomes 20 million for the two years after. And if you then look at investment in defence, it is not in proportion to each other."

title: British forensic science student murders woman in 'Dexter' room
lead: In England, a forensic science student has admitted to murdering a 24-year-old woman after he lured her to a 'murder room' in an Airbnb property. Benjamin Day was obsessed with the television series Dexter, the British public prosecutor says. Last December, Day, then 19 years old, called a sex worker using a disposable phone. He had rented a room in Tividale near Birmingham, which he had set up based on a room in the American series. Dexter is about a forensic expert working for the police who is also a serial killer and knows how to cover his tracks. Shopping list Day covered the room with plastic sheeting and made a "shopping list" that included, among other things, an apron and cleaning products. He stabbed the woman 78 times and wanted to cut her into pieces, but stopped because he had injured himself. After the murder, the student left the property and called the emergency number to ask for medical help for himself. The police noticed that his story did not add up. Later, the Airbnb landlord also called the police, because another tenant had seen blood. After his arrest, Day initially said he had acted in self-defence and had set up the room only to record a Dexter tribute for TikTok. Later he backed down from that and admitted guilt with a grin, writes the BBC. Day will learn on 4 December what his sentence will be. Earlier 'Dexter' murder It is not the first time a Briton seems to have been inspired by the series to commit a murder. In 2014, a 17-year-old boy from England was sentenced to life imprisonment for the murder of his girlfriend, after he had stabbed her and sawed her into pieces in his bedroom.

title: Unrest in Hoogeveen for days, more youths arrested
lead: The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> arrested six people in Hoogeveen this evening, including several minors. There has been unrest in the city centre for days: yesterday there were also eight arrests for misconduct, such as throwing fireworks at passers-by. The police are clearly present in the city centre. Because fireworks bangs were also heard this evening, officers searched young people on the street, RTV <entity id="org:provincie-drenthe">Drenthe</entity> reports. Minor youths. In recent days incidents have regularly occurred in Hoogeveen. These often involve minors who, among other things, ride fatbikes through the centre, intimidate passers-by and set off fireworks and throw them at people. The eight people arrested last night were all minors. In addition, 32 fines were issued and two fatbikes were seized. Earlier, the municipality tried to bring the youths under control by deploying extra cameras and a ban on gatherings. The police remain present in the centre this evening to prevent further escalation.

title: American arrested for helping with school shooting in Canada
lead: Police in the American state of Washington have arrested a 30-year-old woman in connection with a school shooting in Canada in February. An 18-year-old shooter shot her mother and half-brother dead at home, after which she killed five children and a teacher at her former high school in Tumbler Ridge. 25 others were injured. She then took her own life. Tips via online chat The prosecutor in Seattle says that the 30-year-old James Cody Bryant had contact with the shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, for at least six months. According to the prosecutor, Bryant gave Van Rootselaar tips via online chat on how to commit the murders in a way that would have as much impact as possible. "In a corridor people have many ways to escape, for example by hiding behind a corner," Bryant wrote according to the indictment. "A vast open space means large numbers." Bryant also reportedly sent Van Rootselaar money to buy a lighter, with which she could make an explosive. And she gave advice on how the plan could be kept secret, by deleting the online messages, the prosecution says. Snitching The two reportedly got to know each other three years ago via a chat site. The first year there was only sporadic contact because Van Rootselaar reportedly had been committed involuntarily due to psychological problems. In the six months before the attack they were in contact daily. Both the shooter and the accomplice are trans women, but the prosecutors say they have no indications that they sought each other out online for that reason. According to the prosecutor, Bryant tried several more times to change Van Rootselaar's mind. But when Van Rootselaar expressed her concern that Bryant would go "snitching", Bryant said she would not do that. "I know I could save lives or something, but I don't know," she wrote according to the indictment. In the end she indeed did not go to the police. Van Rootselaar did not only have contact with Bryant, but also prepared her act with the help of ChatGPT. The province of British Columbia last month filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, the company behind the AI service. The province claims that the company could have prevented the shooting by raising the alarm with the authorities. Need help? Are you thinking about suicide or worried about someone? Talking helps. You can do so 24/7 for free and anonymously via the chat at www.113.nl or by phone at 113 or 0800-0113.

title: Polder talks with cabinet, which hopes for ideas on the economy and WIA
lead: After months of actions and strikes, employers and employees are meeting the cabinet again today at the Catshuis. Earlier the trade unions walked away, but now that the cuts to the AOW, WIA and WW have been scrapped, they want to talk again. Politicians expect quite a lot from the social partners, in other words 'the polder'. Five questions about a possible social agreement. What is now expected of the polder? "Cooperation with the social partners, society and both chambers is the only way forward," the cabinet writes in the invitation. Ageing, job losses due to artificial intelligence and absence due to illness are named as major social challenges. The polder must think along about the sustainability of social security, the cabinet believes. A plan is also needed for a stronger economy, in other words about the future earning capacity of the Netherlands as described in the Wennink report. It is not a surprising agenda, because the trade unions and employers have already discussed this themselves in recent months, formally and informally, without the cabinet. That economic growth is the best way to safeguard social provisions is agreed by the social partners. They also agree that something must be done about the work incapacity assessments under the WIA. Will there be no cuts to social security at all anymore? Probably yes, but at this moment it cannot yet be said how much. What is clear is that, to get the trade unions back to the table, the minority cabinet has removed the announced cuts to social security entirely from the budget of the Ministry of Social Affairs. That leaves a gap of 2.4 billion euros in the budget. This makes clear that the problem has not yet been solved. "Bills do not disappear by pretending they are not there. There will have to be reform, one way or another," said <entity id="person:eelco-heinen">minister Heinen</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-financien">Financiën</entity> last week during the General Financial Considerations. So the cabinet is counting on the talks in the polder ultimately leading to an agreement with savings. This is especially expected to succeed for the WIA. At the same time, it has not yet been said that these talks will be finished by spring or that they will lead to enough savings to close the budget gap. In that case, the coalition will again discuss among itself in the spring how to solve this and whether and where extra cuts are needed. For now, the budget gap of half (1.2 billion) has in any case been parked with Education. What does the Netherlands gain from such an agreement? The Netherlands has a long tradition of consultation between employers and employees. The Wassenaar Agreement of 1982 is often mentioned as an important historical outcome of polder consultation. The economy was performing poorly, unemployment was high, and the polder eventually agreed on wage restraint. Another example is the 2019 pension agreement, which made a rigorous change to the pension system possible. The advantage of such agreements is that the signatures of employers and employers ensure the plans hold, even if a cabinet falls. It therefore offers a chance to tackle major social or economic problems without the trade unions and employers putting new demands on the table. What do they agree on regarding the WIA? Both employers and employees find that the assessment system for the WIA work incapacity benefit is too complex. Whether you receive a benefit is determined not by the condition but by the amount of income loss. Many errors have been made in calculating this in recent years. And people with a higher income have a greater chance of receiving a benefit. In addition, the waiting list is growing due to a shortage of assessment doctors. Furthermore, employers feel too many Dutch people end up in the WIA. In 2018, the <entity id="org:zbo-uitvoeringsinstituut-werknemersverzekeringen">UWV</entity> still granted 41,400 new WIA applications. In 2025 that was 71,300. The trade unions point out that the Dutch have to keep working a little longer and are more often dropping out before their pension. Employers are also said to do too little to prevent dropping out and, ultimately, work incapacity. Employers and employees previously made agreements on healthy working until retirement and on continuously retraining staff to prevent employees from ending up without work. This yields too little result, the trade unions say. They want employers to be required to take prevention and retraining seriously. Employers, in turn, are now putting continued pay during sickness on the agenda. Following the Wennink report, employers feel they have to pay wages during illness for too long. Sickness absence will therefore be on the agenda, but the social partners differ strongly in their views on how to reduce absence. When would such a social agreement come? Today's meeting seems mainly intended to restart the conversation. The cabinet also wants to discuss a timeline for such a social agreement. Last week Minister Heinen named spring as a "benchmark", but the trade unions are in no hurry. There will be no agreement before Christmas, they say. It could be a matter of months, or perhaps even two years, they indicate. It is also still an open question whether it should become one big agreement. It may also be that separate agreements come on, for example, absence, the labour market and economic growth.

title: Trump calls Putin over death at plague institute, WHO also wants more information
lead: US President Trump plans to call his Russian counterpart Putin "very soon" about the death of a woman at a plague institute in Irkutsk. According to Russian media the woman died of plague, but the authorities deny this and speak of "pneumonia of unknown cause". "A phone call is scheduled, very soon", Trump answered reporters' questions. "We have already been talking about it extensively. Tomorrow we can probably say more." Trump had offered Russia support a day earlier already, should it be needed. A Kremlin spokesperson responded that "mutual support is always appreciated", but did not yet say whether the offer would be taken up. Transparency crucial On Friday a laboratory worker at the anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, which has been doing research into the disease for almost 100 years, died. Russian media wrote that the 28-year-old woman became infected with plague when a test tube broke. The Russian authorities deny this and say the cause of the woman's death has not yet been established. As a precaution, people who had been in contact with her have been placed in quarantine. No further infections have been reported. The World Health Organization WHO has contacted Russian health services to obtain more information. The organisation hopes to get more details about the infection and the Russian approach, and offered to step in where needed. According to the WHO, the current risk assessment is "moderate to low for Irkutsk, low for Russia and particularly low for Europe". WHO chief Tedros stresses that "timely, complete and transparent information under international agreements is essential to clarify conflicting reports and to make an accurate assessment of the health risks". 'No panic, but attention' "Maybe it is nothing, maybe it is bigger than we think, we don't know", said American minister Rubio of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> yesterday. "We are keeping a close eye on it, and I think the whole world is doing so." "There is no reason for panic, but there is reason for attention", he continued. "If something like this escapes, it can move quickly." He did note that currently little travel takes place between Russia and the US. The disease can be treated with antibiotics if detected in time. The American embassy in the United States says it is monitoring the situation closely, but also warns that it has few options to help Americans in Russia, especially outside Moscow. The embassy points out that a negative travel advisory still applies to the whole country for general security reasons.

title: Cabinet wants citizens to have a hybrid heat pump after all
lead: Many people who need a new heating boiler from 2029 will then have to buy a smart hybrid heat pump. The standards are being tightened so that a regular gas-fired central heating boiler no longer meets them. <entity id="person:elanor-boekholt-osullivan">Minister Boekholt-O'Sullivan</entity> of Housing writes to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> that the cabinet sees the hybrid heat pump as an intermediate step on the way to gas-free heating for all buildings by 2050. That is important for meeting the climate targets. In 2022 the Rutte IV cabinet already wanted to make the hybrid heat pump mandatory from 2026, but that plan was scrapped under the Schoof cabinet. PVV, NSC, VVD and BBB mainly felt the costs for households were too high. Experiences positive The current minority cabinet is now dusting off the plan. The coalition agreement states that the hybrid heat pump should become "the new standard". Such a device draws its heat from the outside air and the electricity grid, but on cold days it can also work together with a gas central heating boiler. Hundreds of thousands of households have recently switched to a fully electric heat pump or a hybrid variant. According to the minister, the experiences of many consumers are positive. Purchases are already being encouraged, but a real acceleration of development requires more, said Boekholt. Smart The new standard will only apply when the central heating boiler is replaced, so as long as the existing boiler works it can stay. Residents of apartments and monuments also do not need to switch, as it is often not possible to use a heat pump there. The cabinet would prefer people to switch to a fully gas-free heat pump, but a smart hybrid variant also suffices. 'Smart' means the installation can be set so that it mainly uses electricity at times when demand for electricity is low, as well as the price. That is important to spare the overloaded electricity grid. Hybrid heat pump A hybrid heat pump uses much less gas than a traditional central heating boiler: the saving can rise to 65 percent. The purchase costs are considerably higher, however: quickly 8,000 euros (including installation), compared with 2,000 euros for a central heating boiler. There are subsidy schemes to make purchase more attractive. With these, the costs come to about 6,000 euros. Because of the lower energy bill, according to Vereniging Eigen Huis you earn back a hybrid heat pump in about ten years. The cabinet states that households with a heat pump will also have a lower energy bill in the coming years. Moreover, the investment leads to a considerable increase in the value of the home, Boekholt writes. The minister realises that 6,000 euros is still "terribly much money" for many people. That is why she is announcing it now already, "so you know that when your boiler is due for replacement there is a cost item and that you can take that into account". In the coming period she will work out further how everyone can be enabled to make the purchase. In any case, she wants to offer interest-free loans. Furthermore, Boekholt emphasises that the hybrid heat pump is "the logical successor to the central heating boiler". "Just as we first got the VR boiler with improved efficiency and then the HR boiler with high efficiency."

title: Last active NSC member leaves, does not want to cooperate with Mona Keijzer
lead: European Parliament member Dirk Gotink is ending his membership of Nieuw Sociaal Contract (NSC). With that, the party founded by Pieter Omtzigt loses its last elected representative. Gotink writes on LinkedIn that he does not want to belong to a party that seeks rapprochement with Mona Keijzer. "The choice for a possible cooperation with Project2029 of Mona Keijzer is incomprehensible to me." Keijzer is guest speaker this coming Saturday at NSC's general members' meeting in Breda. She will then take part in a discussion about the party's fundamental principles and starting points. Going it alone <entity id="person:maria-cornelia-gezina-keijzer">Kamerlid Keijzer</entity>, who has sat in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> as a one-person faction since her break with BBB, is founding a new socially conservative movement named Project2029. According to Gotink, he and Keijzer are playing a very different game, "certainly when it comes to Europe". He considers "sowing doubt about the importance of the EU" irresponsible and feels compelled by this to leave. He will continue in the European Parliament as an independent member of the European People's Party (EPP). Swept away NSC won twenty seats in one go in 2023, then joined <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>-Schoof, but withdrew from it. In the elections that followed, the party was swept away. In January party leader Van Hijum stepped down. There is not yet a new leader. The board would work on a relaunch. It has not been said that a cooperation with Project2029 will be considered in that context.

title: ABN Amro slightly less in Dutch State's hands again
lead: The Dutch State is further reducing its stake in ABN Amro. At the moment the State still holds 20.7 percent of the bank, but this will be further reduced to 10.5 percent over the coming period. That is announced by NL Financial Investments (<entity id="org:rwt-stichting-administratie-kantoor-financiele-instellingen-nlfi">NLFI</entity>), which manages the government's stakes in banks and insurers on behalf of <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity>. ABN Amro was bought up during the credit crisis for 16.8 billion euros. <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> wanted to use the intervention to prevent the bank from collapsing. In 2015 the State decided to gradually sell its shares in the bank again. Last July it became known that the stake had meanwhile been reduced to 20.7 percent. For years there was fear that the intervention would cost the Netherlands money. But recently the market value of ABN Amro has risen considerably, so much more money is being earned from selling the shares than was initially thought. There is now even a chance that the State will not lose money on it and will even earn a little. The NLFI is selling the shares very gradually. How long it will take before the stake has been reduced to 10.5 percent cannot be said. The last sales round of shares took about ten months and yielded almost 2.5 billion euros. Ultimately the intention is that the State's stake in ABN Amro will be reduced to 0.

title: Rotterdam opens permanent winter shelter, not only during frost
lead: Rotterdam will provide shelter to homeless people throughout this entire winter. The municipality calls it "a major step" in tackling homelessness. Normally the winter shelter is linked to temperature and only opens when feels-like temperatures fall below freezing. From 1 November there is a permanent place for 150 people in the Overschie district. The winter shelter stays open for five months. Social workers and medical help will be present. The municipality hopes that by letting people stay in one place for longer, it can more easily guide them to a follow-up pathway. At the same location there are also fifty places for labour migrants from the European Union and twenty for people waiting for a home via Centraal Onthaal, the municipal registration point for homeless people. Evening meal: According to the municipality, around two hundred to three hundred people sleep outside in Rotterdam daily. Alderman Astrid Kockelkoren (Homelessness) does not expect all of them to want to use the winter shelter, writes regional broadcaster Rijnmond. When it starts to freeze outside, the basic shelter will be expanded. The opening hours of the shelter in Overschie will also be extended. The location was in previous winters open from 18.00 to 09.00 hours. From next month people can come from 16.00 to 11.00 hours. That should bring more calm. Homeless people also receive an evening meal and breakfast. The shelter is run by the Nico Adriaans Stichting (NAS), a care organisation committed to vulnerable Rotterdammers. Elections: In the municipal council elections last March, the homelessness problem was one of the main themes in Rotterdam. The plan for permanent winter shelter was signed by coalition parties Pro, D66, VVD, CDA and Volt. Opposition parties PvdD, CU, SP and Bij1 also signed. It is part of the Stadsakkoord Dakloosheid, which consists of eleven points to reduce the growing number of homeless people in the city. Permanent shelter: Rotterdam is not the first Dutch municipality to offer permanent shelter in winter. In <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> too, from 1 November, there is space for homeless people for five months. In <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity> homeless people can use the winter shelter from 1 December. That is separate from the extra shelter that is realised when the feels-like temperature falls below zero at night.

title: Bats finally gone from Drenthe primary school, demolition can begin
lead: The bats that have been plaguing an old primary school in the Drenthe village of Eext for months are finally gone. The school spent at least 2 ton trying to get the animals to leave on their own, and has now succeeded. The school building of Prins Willem primary school is outdated and must make way for a new building. But because a colony of protected bats lived in the attic, that could not simply happen. The demolition and new construction have already been postponed several times. The animals may not be chased away or fought, they must move on their own accord. The school had already hung bat boxes in the hope they would go there, but the species that lived there preferred large spaces - such as the attic roof. This spring that roof was therefore rebuilt for 200,000 euros and placed next to the school. The roof had exactly the same angle of slope and orientation to the sun as the existing roof. One-way flap: But the bats did not let themselves be seduced and stayed in the old roof. With the upcoming hibernation, in which moving is no longer on the table at all, the school took action again three weeks ago. On the facade of the old building one-way flaps were installed, a kind of cat flaps through which the bats could get out, but not back in. All other openings of the building were closed by bat experts. Demolition: That worked, says a spokesperson for the municipality of <entity id="org:gemeente-aa-en-hunze">Aa en Hunze</entity> to RTV <entity id="org:provincie-drenthe">Drenthe</entity> . "The bats have all left the school building and are now in the rebuilt roof. We can start demolishing." The demolition is expected to begin this autumn. Construction of the new building starts early next year, and if all goes well pupils can attend lessons in the new school building from the 2028/2029 school year.

title: Interest on student debt rises sharply for a large group of former students
lead: Next year, the interest on student finance and student debt will rise for students and 250,000 former students. For some of them, the interest will rise by almost 1 percentage point, from 2.29 percent to 3.28 percent. How much the interest rises depends on whether you are still studying and under which repayment rules you fall. Most current students have to repay their debt over 35 years. For them, the interest rises much less: from 2.33 percent to 2.70 percent. Most people who have since graduated fall under the 15-year repayment rules. For them, a new interest rate is set every five years. Five years ago they still paid 0 percent interest. Now it is 3.28 percent. Why does the interest differ? The interest on student loans is based on the interest the government pays. The rates differ this much because they are calculated differently. For the 15-year rule there is one reference date, while for the 35-year rule the average interest over a longer period is used. Earlier this week it became known that total student debt has decreased for the first time in a long time. However, the number of graduates with a very high student debt, above 50,000 euros, has increased considerably. This is partly explained by the loan system, which has since been abolished. Voices have long been calling to lower the interest for this group of students, also known as the 'bad luck generation'. D66, VVD and CDA also want this: in their coalition agreement they agreed to set the interest for students at a maximum of 2.5 percent. So far, no plans for this have been made public. <entity id="org:dienst-uitvoering-onderwijs">DUO</entity>, the organisation responsible for student finance, takes a person's income into account when repaying student debt. Those who earn little have to repay less. The debt that remains after a repayment period is ultimately forgiven.

title: French police temporarily stop using stun grenades at schoolchildren's protests
lead: French police will not use stun grenades at the schoolchildren's protests for the coming period, says the Minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, Nuñez. A stun grenade is used to blind or stun people with a loud bang and a flash of light. The decision comes after a 15-year-old boy lost his hand at a demonstration in the city of Lens. The mayor of Wingles, where the boy lives, says the teenager's left hand has been amputated. He also had a transplant on his right hand and suffered injuries to his face and chest. Since last week, protests against problems in education have been held at schools across France. Schoolchildren are demonstrating against, among other things, overdue maintenance of school buildings, classes that are too large, school days that are too long and the teacher shortage in France. Arrested or thrown? It is still unclear exactly what went wrong in Lens. Riot police were called when the demonstration there reportedly turned into riots, according to French authorities. French media, citing a police source, write that riot police threw a stun grenade and that the boy wanted to throw it back. The grenade then reportedly exploded in his hand. Eyewitnesses say the stun grenade was thrown and landed directly in the hand of the 15-year-old. So he would not have picked it up. An investigation has been launched into the incident. The use of stun grenades is being suspended "until the truth has come to light", Nuñez told the French branch of RTL. Multiple incidents This is not the first incident since the protests began. So far 215 schoolchildren have been injured. Another boy, for example, broke his jaw last week when he was hit in the face by a tear gas grenade. That case is also being investigated. Nuñez previously said that eighteen investigations are underway into violent incidents. The minister has called on police to use proportionate force. On the petition platform for the French parliament, a petition has been started to ban the use of weapons and grenades at demonstrations. It has already collected thousands of signatures. Demonstrations announced Today there do not appear to be any large protests planned. Many schools are simply open today. Yesterday French Prime Minister Lecornu said there would be three days without lessons at schools. At that time it was unclear whether schools would follow this. According to the Ministry of Education, lessons at 86 percent of secondary schools continue as normal today. At 528 schools, lessons have been partly or completely suspended. However, it seems the protests will not stop yet. One of the largest unions in France, CGT, said there are plans to continue demonstrating tomorrow.
