The hairdresser's shop on Westhavenkade had also previously been the target of vandalism. Bricks were thrown at the shop window at that time, Rijnmond reported. The reason for the attacks is unclear, but it is being speculated that they could be related to unfair competition. The hairdressers who are targets are said to be charging prices for haircuts that are below the usual rates, the AD wrote earlier this year.

title: How to defeat Russia? NATO's top military officer answers in a rare speech
lead: How does NATO defeat Russia if that country attacks the military alliance? The alliance's military commander gives the answer this afternoon at a security summit in Warsaw. The announcement of his speech promises nothing less than a 'theory of victory' over the Russians. Because the title reads: 'The theory of victory: how do we achieve military success against Russia through deterrence and defence?' According to news site Bloomberg, the speech says that NATO wants to swiftly repel a Russian attack with artificial intelligence and large quantities of drones. Ground troops should also be deployed to stop an invasion and destroy the Russian command structure. Speech live on NOS The speech by the American Supreme Allied Commander of NATO, General Alexus Grynkewich, can be followed live from 13.00 via the NOS app and NOS.nl. NOS correspondents Kysia Hekster (NATO) and Christiaan Paauwe (Central and Eastern Europe) explain in the stream what makes the speech so special. The speech comes at a tense moment. European countries increasingly see 'hybrid attacks' which are suspected to be the work of the Russians. Those attacks are also becoming more serious. They include arson at ammunition depots with weapons for Ukraine, sabotage on the railways, armed or unarmed drones appearing, and hacks. Western security services see the number of attacks increasing very rapidly. Panic is the goal The attacks aim to sow panic and reduce support for Ukraine. For NATO it is difficult to respond to this kind of attack that is not 'serious' enough to strike back fully, as intended in the famous Article 5 of NATO ("an attack on one is an attack on all"). Moreover, it is often difficult to prove that the Russians are indeed behind them. Meanwhile a discussion has broken out about the term 'hybrid attacks'. "We must stop that," says, for example, the foreign minister of Estonia. According to him, these are terror attacks and sabotage attacks that amount to 'a kind of war'. At the headquarters in Brussels there is restraint. We must not let ourselves be provoked, keep a cool head and continue supporting Ukraine, is the thinking. Still, it now seems time for a public NATO answer to the Russians. It comes from the mouth of NATO's military commander Alexus Grynkewich, an American four-star general. As well known as NATO chief <entity id="person:mark-rutte">Mark Rutte</entity> is, the military commander, in jargon Saceur, an abbreviation of Supreme Allied Commander Europe, is usually that anonymous. The highest operational commander of the alliance is always an American, the political head a European. Speech especially remarkable That the Saceur is seeking out the media today makes it especially remarkable, says Eleonora Russell, former head of communications of NATO's military branch. She thinks it is good that Grynkewich is coming out into the open. "Such a widely announced, strategic speech his predecessors never gave. But Grynkewich is different. He says: if I don't speak out, the chance of war increases. He has good relations with the White House. What he is going to say has Trump's support." In this way the alliance also hopes to show that the American president is "fully committed" to NATO, as Rutte keeps emphasising. Trump himself often sows doubt about his involvement. For example, he said that NATO countries that do not contribute enough to the alliance could, in his view, be attacked. This week he also concluded an agreement with President Putin for the import of large quantities of diesel oil, intended to bring down pump prices before the mid-term elections in America. According to the British newspaper Financial Times, the American president also threatens to halt weapons deliveries to Ukraine through a NATO programme if that country continues attacking Russian energy facilities. Cooperation, not deterrence These are examples of cooperation with Moscow instead of deterrence. Yet this afternoon's speech must reassure NATO countries and make clear that the alliance is ready to strike back if necessary. According to Russell, this 'theory of victory' is not NATO's first, but it is a first that it is partly presented at the request of the allies. In Moscow and Beijing the speech will undoubtedly be listened to with interest. But is it wise to put such a NATO playbook with all the ins and outs out into the open? "He of course will not do that," says Russell. She thinks Moscow will use the story regardless as 'proof' that the alliance is out for war. The speech will emphasise exactly the opposite: NATO is a defensive alliance that responds to an attack. Deterring the Russians is the purpose of the theory of victory, so that it never has to become practice.

title: D66 wants lower threshold for speaking with child when child abuse is suspected
lead: Governing party D66 wants children to be spoken with quickly when there are serious signals of child abuse, where necessary without consultation with the parents. That is stated in a private member's bill by MPs <entity id="person:marijke-synhaeve">Marijke Synhaeve</entity> and Hanneke van der Werf. The proposal is being published online today so that organisations can respond. "What we want is for children to be better heard, seen and helped", says Synhaeve. In recent years it became clear in serious cases that the child was not heard. Examples are the girl who was tortured in Stadskanaal and the foster girl in Vlaardingen, who was also seriously abused. In both cases, signals from the children or their environment were not picked up properly. Specialist bodies such as the Children's Ombudsman have long been calling for the voice of the child to be heard more when abuse is suspected. Only now after parental consent. MP Synhaeve says she has spoken with many victims who said they were not listened to. With the 'child-first law', the MPs want to ensure that children get help quickly and do not have to tell their story to many different people. Most importantly, they can be heard without parental consent if the parents may be involved in the abuse. Currently, care providers may in principle only make contact with the child if the parents or guardians give consent. Only under strict conditions can this be deviated from. But this is complicated and does not happen often. Barnahus-model. The bill states that the method can be used when there are signals of criminal offences. The approach is to apply to children both within and outside youth care. Within 48 hours a special team must hear the child and come up with a plan for protection, care and, where necessary, criminal prosecution. The team involved must consist of people with different areas of expertise in medical care, youth care, safety and justice. This approach is based on the Barnahus-model, which is already used in many other countries. Barnahús is Icelandic for 'children's house'. It is a child-friendly, multidisciplinary approach for child victims and witnesses of violence, sexual abuse or exploitation of children. Better cooperation. Synhaeve is not worried that the approach will lead to much extra work or more out-of-home placements. According to her, it will instead lead to agencies cooperating better and help being available more quickly for children and families who need it. Once the responses from organisations are in, the bill, possibly in amended form, will be submitted to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>.

title: Bricks without gas kilns? Full power grid stands in the way of more sustainable industry
lead: Many regional industrial companies cannot make their operations more sustainable. For the production of glass, cardboard and stone, for example, they often use large machines that consume a lot of energy. In the coming years these must be replaced, and companies would preferably do so by switching to electric machines. But there is too little room on the power grid. That is stated in the report by Cluster6, a partnership of regional energy-intensive industrial companies in manufacturing, waste processing and the Ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-kgg">Klimaat en Groene Groei</entity>. The brickworks of the company Wienerberger are also affiliated with the partnership. Some 70 million bricks and paving stones are made there each year, still largely with the help of gas kilns. But if it is up to director Jasper Vos, those will quickly become electric appliances. One of the factories is on the waiting list for a heavier power connection. "We were promised that there would be room somewhere before 2030, but the question is whether that will actually happen," he says at the location in Pannerden, north-east of Nijmegen. Grid congestion First of all, why is there not enough capacity on the power grid? That is because in recent years companies and households have switched to electricity to a great extent, but the underground cables were not designed for that. This creates grid congestion; in the morning and evening demand for power is much higher than during the day and at night. The grid operator takes these 'peaks' into account and therefore cannot grant every new request. In any case, not before the cables can handle it. Therefore grid operators are reinforcing the power grid. The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets introduced measures two years ago to resolve shortages on the power grid. This means that socially important institutions such as schools and hospitals get priority on the grid. Companies that help reduce grid congestion, such as solar and wind parks or companies installing large batteries, also get priority on the waiting list. Industrial companies end up at the very bottom of the waiting list. Interim solutions Because the waiting list is tied to a region, companies in a region where there is little 'competition' on the power grid may get a connection immediately, while companies elsewhere have to wait for years. "Take for example a glass factory that wants to become sustainable in 2030. If the grid operator tells it that there is only room in 2034, the factory has to bridge that gap," says Barbara Verwayen, who represents the regional industrial companies on behalf of Cluster6. According to her, temporary, local generation of electricity at the companies could offer an interim solution. "If that can be done sustainably, then that is terrific, with sun, wind and batteries. If it cannot be done sustainably, we will have to temporarily generate extra electricity with gas turbines." In this way companies could, while waiting for a heavier power connection, still start investing in electric machines. But more is needed for that than money alone, says Verwayen. "Laws and regulations, the legal framework, granting of permits, all those things." Resistance Grid operators have been working on reinforcing the power grid for some time. To do so, they are building around a hundred high-voltage stations and other power infrastructure in the coming years. Finding a suitable location is often complicated. Protected flora and fauna or proximity to a Natura 2000 area can make building a new station impossible. In addition, operators often encounter resistance from local residents who would rather not see an industrial high-voltage station in their 'backyard'. This causes delays and uncertainty about the expansion of the power grid in the Netherlands. "Due to uncertainty about a power connection, investments are leaking away abroad," says Vos of the Wienerberger brickworks. "You look over the river here to Germany. Similar companies in neighbouring countries do have access to electricity. If we do not get that certainty and space, the survival of this type of company in the Netherlands is at stake."

title: Strike in Belgium over cuts to public services: fewer trains, VRT also on strike
lead: In Belgium, trade unions are protesting again today against announced cuts by <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity>. The strike day will affect schools, public transport and waste collection. Staff at the Flemish broadcaster VRT are also laying down their work. The strike is an initiative of the socialist union ACOD. The protest is aimed at the cuts to public services announced by the regering-De Wever. Tomorrow the prime minister was due to explain the budget choices in his State of the Union, but due to the absence of a budget agreement that has been postponed. His government has been in crisis since this weekend, because the coalition parties cannot agree on that budget. Rail: The strike at the Belgian railway company NMBS began yesterday evening and until 10.00 p.m. this evening fewer trains will run. This also affects train travel to and from the Netherlands, NS reports. Travellers are advised to check the journey planner before departure. Fewer buses, trams and metros are also running in Belgium. Staff at broadcaster VRT are also laying down their work. The broadcaster still has to cut 10 million euros, on top of an earlier announced round of cuts. Many TV broadcasts are being scrapped, news bulletins have been shortened and on the radio there will mostly be music, the broadcaster reports. On 9 November a decision will be taken on further actions. Riots: Last Friday a strike in Brussels against cuts to social security ended in riots, after hundreds to thousands of masked youths had mixed in among the demonstrators. They threw stones and fireworks at the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. The police said the disturbances were not linked to the union action. At least 110 people were arrested. A day earlier a ban on gatherings was announced in Liège, because of education protests that had got out of hand in that city. Those protests have partly spilled over from France, where since last month demonstrations have been held against, among other things, the poor state of school buildings and the teacher shortage.

title: Crash between crane and bus causes havoc in Nijmegen
lead: In Nijmegen a bus was damaged this morning in an accident with a crane truck. A passenger was injured and taken to hospital, Omroep Gelderland reports. The accident happened this morning around 07.00 hours on the Industrieweg, on the western edge of Nijmegen. While braking for a roundabout, the ballast of a crane truck hit the side of a bus carrying passengers. An advertising column and several lampposts along the road were also struck. Several emergency services, including several officers and an ambulance, went to the scene. A bus passenger who was sitting at the back of the bus was taken to hospital by ambulance staff. The other passengers were transported to Nijmegen by smaller buses. Havoc The collision caused havoc. A large part of the Industrieweg towards the centre of Nijmegen is strewn with debris from the advertising column, lampposts and glass. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> is investigating the cause.

title: SPD leader Bas steps down after attacks from coalition partner CDU in 'difficult time'
lead: Bärbel Bas, co-chair of the German governing party SPD, has unexpectedly stepped down. She also gives up her post as minister of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-sociale-zaken-en-werkgelegenheid">Sociale Zaken en Werkgelegenheid</entity>. The departure follows a death in the family and ongoing attacks on her personally. "After the death of my stepdaughter I realised I need more time to process the grief", Bas writes in a statement. Precisely in this "personally difficult time" the attacks on her have increased, she continues. "Also from the ranks of our coalition partner." According to the other co-chair, vice chancellor Lars Klingbeil, boundaries have been crossed. The attacks are "unseemly" and "poison the political culture", he says. "I am worried that we are losing empathetic figures in politics." Women in particular are targets of such attacks, hatred and incitement, according to Klingbeil. Bas belonged to the heart of the German government, but as minister repeatedly clashed with federal chancellor Merz and his CDU/CSU. The Christian Democrats want to reduce social contributions and regularly came up against Bas, who belongs to the left wing of the social democratic SPD. When Merz claimed that the current welfare state is unsustainable, Bas spoke of "bullshit". In recent weeks the CDU/CSU criticised Bas for the slow implementation of controversial pension plans, which are unpopular within the SPD. Bas would have deliberately slowed the reforms, while it was known within the coalition that there was a death in her family. Sour relationship The attacks on Bas are heavily criticised by SPD members. "The attacks by the CDU, despite her personally difficult situation, were inhumane and reckless", writes the influential SPD member Manuela Schwesig, state premier of Mecklenburg-Voor-Pommeren. Party colleague Bernd Rützel speaks of unacceptable attacks, both by CDU members and by "certain media". Within the CDU/CSU, Bas's outburst is in fact seen as inappropriate. Focus Online writes that the parliamentary group stayed away from criticism precisely because of her situation. An insider told the news site it was a "cheap kick when she is down". According to the Süddeutsche Zeitung, Merz did complain about Bas's absence, including to journalists. It shows how sour the relationship between the governing parties has become. Both parties feel the other is obstructing agreed reforms. Merz recently blocked the planned sugar tax, a project of SPD vice chancellor Klingbeil. On the other side, the SPD has objections to pension reforms. The election of a parliamentary president from the radical right-wing AfD in the state of Saksen-Anhalt, with the help of CDU votes, also led to tension. The SPD demands an explanation of this and wants the coalition partner to act against those who voted for it. Conversely, the CDU is pressuring the SPD not to govern with Die Linke in the state of Berlin, a party that the Christian Democrats consider antisemitic. Negotiations on healthcare reforms became so tense that federal president Steinmeier had to intervene, because he feared the government would collapse. Both parties, however, have no interest in a coalition break-up or new elections. The CDU/CSU in particular has fallen into free fall in the polls in recent weeks. Merz critic as successor Bas's ministerial post will be taken over by Alexander Schweitzer, former premier of the state of <entity id="org:waterschap-van-rijnland">Rijnland</entity>-Palts. In the past week he openly criticised Merz, who "does not deliver" and governs with a "cold neoliberal spirit of the 1990s". He also sneered that the CDU does not convincingly support Merz. With Schweitzer in this important post, the government once again has an SPD member who takes a critical stance towards the CDU's reform plans. At the same time there is little room to tinker with the agreements already concluded. It is now up to federal chancellor Merz to keep the squabbling coalition together. After the defeats in recent state elections, there was much speculation about his resignation. He stayed on, but with diminished authority within the party. He has tied his fate to carrying out the reforms. The party leadership met today to discuss how the CDU should proceed. Later today Merz will hold a press conference on this.

title: Dismissed dentist drives into dental practice in Belgium out of revenge
lead: In Belgium a dismissed dentist drove his car into a dental practice out of revenge. The driver was slightly injured. He was taken in by police for questioning. According to the Flemish broadcaster VRT, the Romanian man drove his Porsche through the rear of the building in Stekene in East Flanders at around 22.30 hours last night. The driver drove through the glass entrance door of the waiting room, put the car in reverse and then drove into the practice once more. The rear of the building was badly damaged. It took hours for the fire brigade to clear the damage and close the windows and doors. VRT reports that the man worked at the practice but had been dismissed. Nothing has been made public about the reason for his dismissal.

title: Cabinet wants to make it easier for zoos to improve enclosures
lead: There must be new rules for zoos, believes <entity id="person:silvio-erkens">staatssecretaris Erkens</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-landbouw-visserij-voedselzekerheid-en-natuur">Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur</entity>. Zoos that want to renew now face too many extra rules and permits, he believes. Whereas zoos that leave everything as it is have no trouble at all, precisely because they do not innovate. "Zoos have been a beloved outing for young and old for ages", writes Erkens in a letter to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. "At the same time, over the years we have come to attach more value to animal welfare. It is therefore important that zoos keep up with the times." At the moment zoos still have permits for an indefinite period. Only zoos that want to innovate face new tests and the associated costs. A zoo that never changes anything can go on for years without running into rules. Erkens wants to change that. No flexibility Animal care manager Tjerk ter Meulen of zoo Artis in Amsterdam cites as an example the stones in an aquarium. For a permit application, all of them must be marked on a floor plan, including size and weight, he says. "That gives us no flexibility to change them again when the fish need it. Of course we want to constantly respond to the needs and welfare of the animals. And if we then have to apply for a new permit for the enclosure every time, that of course makes things very difficult."

title: Misconduct reported at Utrecht nursing home: 'She simply hasn't been showered for a year'
lead: Relatives of residents of a care centre in <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity> sound the alarm with RTV Utrecht about the conditions on a nursing ward. They say residents are poorly cared for and often left to their own devices. The psychogeriatric ward of Nieuw Tamarinde in Overvecht houses around twenty elderly people who have some form of dementia. Nieuw Tamarinde is part of care institution Careyn. It is active in the municipalities of <entity id="org:gemeente-stichtse-vecht">Stichtse Vecht</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-de-ronde-venen">De Ronde Venen</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-woerden">Woerden</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-oudewater">Oudewater</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-montfoort">Montfoort</entity>, Utrecht and Zeist. RTV Utrecht spoke with several relatives of residents, who wish to remain anonymous. They describe the problems that are occurring on the ward. For example, there is said to be poor care, a lack of hygiene and problems with administering medication. According to the relatives, staff are often nowhere to be seen. 'Not showered for a year' Two women describe the lack of care for their aunt: "She stank at one point. Her nails were very long and there was faeces under them. She was wearing dirty clothes, greasy hair and no mouth care had been done." RTV Utrecht has viewed the aunt's file. Staff members write in it how the woman is doing and what they have done. For example, a carer writes on 4 May this year that "madam" has not been showered for a year because she "resists". The plan is now to wash the woman with two people from now on, so that she can resist less. "She simply hasn't been showered for a year," says her niece indignantly. "She would not have wanted that." 'My mother's dentures were stuck fast' Another woman describes the situation with her husband. "I went there every day. At 9.30 he would be sitting in his wheelchair with greasy hair and black nails," she says. "Then they would pay attention to it and then it would go well for a while." According to a fourth woman, her mother's dentures are not being cleaned. "Her dentures were stuck fast," she says. She describes how a staff member forcefully pulled the dentures out of her mother's mouth. "Her dentures hadn't come out for months." Temporary agency staff The relatives have complained several times to Careyn's management, but so far, they state, little has changed. "It goes well for a bit when you say something about it, and then it's wrong again," says one of them. Careyn's management acknowledges the problems and attributes them to staff shortages. In a complaints mediator's report it can be read: "Every time people drop out again, which partly undoes the improvements." Many temporary agency workers work on the ward, and according to the relatives that is where the problem lies. "A number of permanent staff are really very kind and good, but they are often not there," says a relative. Inspection reports Care institution Careyn informs RTV Utrecht in a written response that it is aware of the relatives' concerns and says it has taken measures to improve the situation. "We have also organised family evenings to listen to what is going on, to discuss concerns and to look together at what needs to be better." The care institution acknowledges that "things have not gone well". "The measures we have put in place have not yet led to the improvement that is needed on all points. We must also face that." The <entity id="org:inspectie-gezondheidszorg-en-jeugd">Inspectie Gezondheidszorg en Jeugd</entity> tells RTV Utrecht that seven reports have been received since the beginning of 2025. The inspectorate cannot say anything about the content of the reports or who made them. The inspectorate does not want to say whether an investigation into the ward will follow.

title: New arrests for fatal shooting incident at Vierdaagsefeesten Nijmegen
lead: The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has arrested two new suspects in the investigation into the fatal shooting during the Vierdaagsefeesten in Nijmegen. They are a 19-year-old man from Amsterdam and a 21-year-old man from Hoorn. On Tuesday 21 July, at around 22.00 hours, an 18-year-old man from Rotterdam was shot dead on Graafseweg. This happened not far from the Vierdaagsefeesten, which were underway in the city at that moment. That same evening, an 18-year-old fellow city resident was arrested. He was released again a day later and has not been a suspect since, reports Omroep Gelderland . The police have since investigated the shooting incident and what preceded it. "This has now resulted in two arrests", the police report. The men are suspected of involvement in the shooting incident. The motive for the shooting is still being investigated. The police therefore are not currently sharing any further information about what the two are specifically suspected of.

title: Minister Hermans scraps 13-week scan for pregnant women from 2028
lead: Pregnant women will no longer be able to use a 13-week scan from 1 January 2028. The current experiment with the scan to detect congenital abnormalities will not be continued, Minister Hermans of Health writes to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. Last month the <entity id="org:gezondheidsraad">Gezondheidsraad</entity> advised against introducing the 13-week scan as a standard part of maternity care. The results of the scan did not always turn out to be correct; sometimes women were referred unnecessarily, while relatively many abnormalities were missed. The Gezondheidsraad concluded that the benefits do not currently outweigh the disadvantages. Hermans largely follows that advice, but goes one step further than the Gezondheidsraad. The council had still argued for further research to use the scan in such a way that the benefits would outweigh the disadvantages. But the minister is not keen on that. Unnecessary anxiety. "Although <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> takes the possibilities for improving the protocol seriously, there currently also appear to be many disadvantages to offering the 13-week scan again within a research setting", writes Hermans. She especially does not want to expose pregnant women again to unnecessary anxiety if the result turns out to be a false alarm. That means the 13-week scan will disappear on 1 January 2028. The research has been offered since 2021 as part of a scientific study, alongside the usual 20-week scan. The idea behind it was that parents with a scan in the thirteenth week of pregnancy have more time to prepare for a child who needs a lot of care or for a possible abortion. In her letter to the House, Hermans writes that she does want to examine the entire chain of prenatal screening. In doing so, she wants to look at how the current system, with scans and the NIPT blood test to detect genetic abnormalities, can be improved. If scientific developments give cause for it, she may ask the Gezondheidsraad again for advice on the 13-week scan.

title: Rail staff talk about suicide: 'standing talking to her for 1,5 hours'
lead: Start the conversation: that is the message of a new campaign for suicide prevention on the railways. Each year around 200 people die in the Netherlands in a collision with a train. Attempted suicides are far more common still. Train drivers, conductors and ProRail employees are now speaking out with their stories in a campaign by 113 and the railway companies. In this way they hope to contribute to reducing the number of suicides. NS head conductor Glenda (41) "I have now been head conductor for 8,5 years. In that period I have experienced one suicide and found perhaps twenty suicidal people. On the tracks, around the station, on the platform. Sometimes it happens very often in a row, sometimes not at all for a year. The first time I experienced it, we received an emergency call 'suicidal person'. After we had stood still for twenty minutes, we got permission to drive again. We were about two kilometres on our way when the driver paged me: 'There is someone in front of my train, can you come forward?' The driver said: 'She is a very young girl, maybe it is better if you go outside.' I then climbed out of the train. She was standing right in front of the train, with her arms wide, and shouted very loudly: 'Make sure he drives, make sure he drives.' I talked to her for about an hour and a half. Eventually she climbed into the train, we drove on and handed her over to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. I have learned to recognise behaviour that is not understood, for example when it is very cold outside and someone is standing there in a T-shirt. I also now know how to deal with it. Do ask that direct question about suicide. If you are off the mark, someone will understand that it was asked with the best intentions. During rush hour I once saw a person standing completely still. Everyone walked around them. Something in me said: this is not right. I went over to them and took them out of the crowd. I did not go into their world until I asked: 'Are you here because you wanted to jump in front of the train?' Then I pulled her out of that daze and she said: 'Yes, that is what I came here to do.'" Incident responder at ProRail Dennis Heijne (34) "We are alerted to animals on the tracks, but also to people with behaviour that is not understood. When there is a collision we receive an alert. As team leader I then select the men and women who make sure the passengers of NS or Arriva can continue as quickly as possible. The number of collisions I have experienced is already getting close to 190. I always find the number a bit confronting to mention. And we have not even got to near-collisions or people around the tracks. You have to be able to deal with that, be able to hold conversations. Otherwise you cannot do this job. We are retrained several times a year. How can you share things? How do you talk about 'I'? It also happens several times a day that we prevent suicides. Then we can make sure people get the right help, if it has not yet been started. It may be that someone with behaviour that is not understood is seen on ProRail cameras, or by bystanders. We then go looking straight away, together with the police. To start a conversation, I first say who I am: Dennis from ProRail. Then I look for something to talk about, which can be something simple: 'I see you have an iPhone.' I want to make a connection, to get someone out of the danger zone. To a bench, away from that level crossing." 113 Are you thinking about suicide or worried about someone? Talking about it helps and can be done anonymously via the chat on www.113.nl or by phone on 113 or 0800-0113.

title: EU countries hold off on a hard response after US sanctions against the Court
lead: The European Union is for now choosing the diplomatic route to keep the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague standing. Harsh measures against the American sanctions against the court are not coming for now. That is the outcome of a meeting of the ministers of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> of the EU countries in Luxembourg. "The most important thing is to engage in dialogue and do everything to protect the court," said <entity id="person:tom-berendsen">minister Berendsen</entity> of Buitenlandse Zaken after the meeting. Belgium would have preferred to take a harder stance against the American sanctions, but does not get sufficient support. Last Friday the American government announced sanctions against the Court. The US is an opponent of the ICC. It does not recognise the court and demands that the ICC not prosecute American nationals. The arrest warrant against Israeli prime minister Netanyahu also led to great anger among Americans. After the sanctions take effect next April, it will be prohibited for American citizens, companies and organisations to do business with the ICC. Organisations outside the US also face sanctions if they cooperate with the court. Earlier, sanctions were already imposed on individual judges and prosecutors at the International Criminal Court. Unacceptable The EU countries called the sanctions unacceptable on Friday. They did stress, however, that the six-month period before the sanctions take effect still offers the chance to engage in talks with the United States. Belgium called today for doing more than just talking by now instructing companies to ignore the American sanctions. European rules offer that possibility. The Netherlands, like the majority of EU countries, wants to keep that option in reserve, partly out of fear that the conflict with the Americans over the Court will otherwise escalate, with possibly major financial consequences for companies. According to Belgian minister Prevot, a firm signal is precisely needed because some companies that now work with the Court are "preventively withdrawing their support." Minister Berendsen could not confirm that this is actually happening. He does see that there are concerns among companies. He therefore finds it important to engage in talks with companies, and to show "that they have full support to continue their work for the court". Red line? In the coming months it will become clear what negotiations will yield. The Americans want the court to no longer be able to prosecute American nationals. Experts stress that such a concession would jeopardise the functioning of the court. "If you grant immunity to residents of one country for the most serious international crimes, then you not only undermine the functioning of the court, but the entire international legal order," said professor of International criminal law Marieke de Hoon on Friday to Nieuwsuur. According to minister Berendsen, the independent functioning of the court is of crucial importance. Whether the American demand is therefore a red line he does not want to say, however: "It is not up to the Netherlands to determine what we can and cannot grant. That is up to the more than 120 countries that are affiliated with the Court". Greenland deal The hope is to still be able to convince the Americans in the coming months to lift the sanctions, without the functioning of the court suffering as a result. In Brussels the Greenland deal is mentioned as an example of how the Americans could still come round. Meanwhile, preparations are also continuing in case the Americans do actually impose the sanctions. In the coming months the countries that participate in the International Criminal Court will use the ICC to protect it as much as possible against the sanctions. They want to do this, among other things, by working with companies and banks that have no ties to the US at all. At an EU summit later this week in Brussels, the heads of government of the member states will also discuss the American sanctions with each other.

title: Other (online) supermarkets are busier due to problems at Albert Heijn
lead: Due to the problems at Albert Heijn, other supermarket chains are busier. A spokesperson for Jumbo says that chain is already scaling up. Jumbo already sees an increase in online orders. The company cannot yet say whether more people are also coming to the stores because shelves are empty at some Albert Heijn branches. "We have to anticipate higher demand. If this lasts longer at Albert Heijn, there will definitely be a gap, of course. That is what we at Jumbo are trying to fill as well as possible." Jumbo says it is also in contact with the CBL, the trade organisation for supermarkets, about the situation. The chain wishes Albert Heijn much strength. "It is really tough for them", the spokesperson said. Stepping in: At online supermarket Picnic too, more is being ordered. "Since this morning we have seen an increase in the number of orders for tomorrow", says a spokesperson. "If it continues like this, we will end up with a few thousand extra orders, which is why we are currently scaling up our delivery capacity." Picnic says it hopes for Albert Heijn that the problems will be resolved quickly. "But if necessary, we can step in over the coming days." Trade organisation CBL says it is certainly thinking about what to do if Albert Heijn branches cannot be supplied for a longer period. "We are keeping an eye on it and of course we are thinking about it, but it is still a little early", says a spokesperson. "The Netherlands has a supermarket landscape that can absorb quite a bit. Our call is: just do your shopping as you normally would, there is no reason for panic." Customers at an Albert Heijn branch in Zaandam saw many empty shelves in the store: Albert Heijn is by far the largest supermarket chain in the Netherlands, with a market share last year of around 38 percent, according to research agency NielsenIQ. Jumbo follows with around 20 percent. The share of Albert Heijn parent company Ahold Delhaize fell today on the Amsterdam stock exchange by 2.8 percent, while the AEX index rose by about 0.4 percent. The ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-landbouw-visserij-voedselzekerheid-en-natuur">Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur</entity> says the situation is worrying. "The problems underline the importance of a stronger and more resilient food system. It is good that Ahold's stores are open and that hard work is being done on a solution. The ministry is closely monitoring the situation and is in contact." Incident: Albert Heijn itself took all kinds of IT systems offline yesterday afternoon due to a 'cybersecurity incident'. Since then the website has not been working, you cannot order online, and several distribution centres of the chain are at a standstill. As a result, stores can be supplied less well and empty shelves are appearing here and there. What exactly is going on, and whether malicious actors have broken into Albert Heijn's systems, is still unclear.

title: End looms for Seal Centre as costly new building and setbacks deliver the final blow
lead: The Pieterburen Seal Centre, which recently moved into the Wadden Sea World Heritage Centre, is threatening to go bankrupt within two weeks. The centre has been struggling with financial problems for some time. These worsened further last week and now the end is really near, says the board. The immediate reason for the announcement is the loss of financial support that had been counted on. The centre says talks about that support were held with the municipality <entity id="org:gemeente-het-hogeland">Het Hogeland</entity>, which Lauwersoog falls under, and the <entity id="org:provincie-groningen">provincie Groningen</entity>. On Thursday they indicated they see no role for themselves, according to a statement from the centre. "We are shocked and saddened." If the centre does go bankrupt, forty people will lose their jobs. The care of sick and orphaned seals would also stop. Seal Centre and Wadden Sea World Heritage Centre The Pieterburen Seal Centre moved into the new Wadden Sea World Heritage Centre in Lauwersoog last year. Along with the Seal Centre, an interactive exhibition and research facilities are based there. The Seal Centre moved to the new location at the beginning of last year. The new building turned out more expensive than expected, and there were several setbacks. Not all bills have been paid yet. At the same time, income is falling short. This consists of donations and entrance tickets. Reserves are depleted, so the deficit keeps growing. It now stands at nearly 3 million euros. "There is still a small hope of a miracle to bridge this amount," says the centre. The board also admits its own part: "In hindsight we may have been too optimistic about visitor development and about addressing setbacks in time." Started out as a crèche The Pieterburen Seal Centre was founded in 1971. It became known as the Zeehondencrèche; most of the animals taken in there were orphaned young seals. From 2006 to 2014 the centre bore the name of its founder, Lenie 't Hart. She stepped down as director in 2012. Two years later she left the centre entirely after a dispute over policy.

title: Major cyber incident at Albert Heijn: 'You don't just take measures like these lightly'
lead: Cybersecurity experts consider it very plausible that someone has broken into the systems of Albert Heijn. Since Sunday afternoon, the online systems of the supermarket chain have been taken offline as a precaution, which is causing major problems in the stores. Albert Heijn does not want to say whether there has been a hack and for now itself speaks of a digital security incident. "Such a large organisation does not just take major measures of this kind lightly," says cybersecurity expert Joey Fennis. "If malicious actors have turned the key in the front door lock, they have probably also looked inside and viewed or taken data." Fennis says that similar measures are taken when that happens. As a result of the outage, Albert Heijn's systems are unavailable, online orders cannot be delivered and some distribution centres are at a standstill, leaving stores with empty shelves. According to Fennis, the top of the company must give permission to take this kind of measure. "Apparently the concern is so great that it reminds me of the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> last year." The OM was hacked at the time via a vulnerability in a program that employees use to work from home. 'Outages usually don't last that long' The fact that drastic action has been taken also leads cybersecurity expert Pim Takkenberg to suspect that there is more going on. "It seems quite clear that a malicious actor has been in the system. Albert Heijn has preventively shut down a number of systems, which is very common to prevent further damage when someone is in your systems," he says on Nieuwsuur. "An outage usually doesn't last that long." Customers at an Albert Heijn branch in Zaandam saw many empty shelves in the store: If a criminal group is behind the outage, according to Takkenberg they are usually after money. "They try to hack systems, steal data and then threaten to publish it if you don't pay. Perhaps a group will come forward later." According to him, it could be a state actor such as Russia, or so-called 'hacktivists' with some kind of ideological aim. But Takkenberg considers it most plausible that a criminal group is responsible. "I think there is no Russian state actor involved in the Netherlands, because all the signals I am seeing now are of a different order of magnitude, although I cannot rule it out. It seems unlikely to me that this belongs to a Russian state actor. This incident fits much more the pattern of criminal groups," said the cybersecurity expert. Fennis fears for customers' data, because those systems have also gone offline. "Just like with Flink, they may be after personal data." An unknown group of hackers broke into that grocery delivery service. Customers were digitally extorted. According to cybersecurity expert Eward Driehuis, it may also be that Albert Heijn itself has found a vulnerability in its system. "If that is not easy to fix, they may be closing the digital doors as a precaution." "What does become clear is how dependent we are on IT and the cyber domain, including for people who do not work with it daily," says Driehuis. "That becomes very concrete now that you can't do your grocery shopping. It is, however, a good eye-opener for people." Because of the outage, Albert Heijn branches are increasingly running out of supplies. Throughout the day, photos came in of stores without stock; fresh products in particular are missing. Meanwhile, other supermarket chains are seeing an increase in orders. Number of days? According to Fennis, it cannot be said how long the problems will last. "That depends on whether they were in time. The question is how far any criminals have got and how long they have been able to carry on, but that is still speculation for now. The investigation will have to show that." "Albert Heijn only communicated about the outage this morning, even though it had been going on for some time. In the best case, I think it will take a number of days."

title: Veilig Thuis reporting point sounds alarm: 'We can no longer handle the work'
lead: A report of domestic violence or child abuse often ends up in a big pile. For years it takes too long before action is taken. Criticism from outside was already there, but now Veilig Thuis itself is sounding the alarm. This is because the number of advice requests and reports keeps rising, situations are becoming more complex, and there are shortages everywhere in care. Each year, tens of thousands of situations in which people may be being abused are picked up too late. According to the organisation, the only solution is for more money to come from the government. Veilig Thuis is the gatekeeper in tackling domestic violence and child abuse. The reporting point gives advice and investigates reports. Especially that investigation takes a lot of time, because people have to be spoken to or information has to be requested from the GP or school. More and more reports. Year after year the number of reports grows. Veilig Thuis is glad about this, because there is more attention for signs of possible abuse. At the same time, there are too many to pick them all up. Last year it concerned 136,000 reports. For just over 90,000 of those reports the organisation was not yet involved with the family, for the others it was. A report must be picked up within five days, the law says. That often does not happen. In recent years about half of the reports have been picked up later. People now have to wait an average of about two months. In some cases it is longer than half a year. "And the outlook for this year gives no hope," says Ida Ouweneel of the board of the Landelijk Netwerk Veilig Thuis. "Normally the waiting list gets slightly smaller in summer, that has not happened now. In autumn there are usually only more reports. We are not getting through it, it can't go on like this anymore." "We do screen all reports that come in," Ouweneel continues. "If there is acute unsafety, there is no waiting list and we pick up the report right away." Abuse in <entity id="org:gemeente-stadskanaal">Stadskanaal</entity>. The inspectorate has been sounding the alarm about waiting times for years. Lawyers also warned when it became known that in Stadskanaal a 6-year-old girl had been seriously abused. Despite reports to Veilig Thuis, the abuse was able to continue. "At this moment we cannot guarantee that we can pick up all signs of unsafety in time," says Ouweneel. "That worries us greatly." Colinda Guiljam, employee at Veilig Thuis in <entity id="org:provincie-zeeland">Zeeland</entity>, also sees that the pile of reports is growing. "Every day when I boot up the computer, I see the number of reports getting bigger. At the start of this year it was just over 30 reports on the waiting list in Zeeland, now it is nearly 400 reports." Stalled youth care. "An example of such a situation on the waiting list is someone who hears a lot of screaming and yelling of a child from the neighbours," explains Guiljam. "There is a suspicion of child abuse, but you don't know more at that moment. Because of the big increase in other crisis situations, it takes longer than you would like to get clarity about the situation of such a child." Not only the number of reports is rising, the type of situations is also changing, Guiljam sees. "If domestic violence or child abuse is no longer detected early, such a situation becomes harder." Not only Veilig Thuis is getting stuck. In youth care there are shortages and waiting lists everywhere. Children and young people in a vulnerable situation do not get the help they need in time. That in turn leads to more reports at Veilig Thuis. "We are passing reports around," says Ouweneel. "The waiting list at our end is a result of youth care getting stuck. There has to be a turnaround, in which help is brought in much faster." Turnaround set in motion. Five years ago such a plan came about, from the sector, the national government and municipalities. It focuses on more cooperation and must provide an answer to the many different youth care organisations. "We are working on that turnaround, but there is now no money set aside for it at all," says Ouweneel. "We really need that to invest. Besides that, we need money to hire extra people in the short term. 70 million euros is needed for the coming years from <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>." <entity id="person:mirjam-sterk">Minister Sterk</entity> says in a response that it is important to map out where the bottlenecks at Veilig Thuis come from. She will soon talk with aldermen, the Vereniging Nederlandse Gemeenten and Veilig Thuis to see what is needed. Whether extra money will really come, she does not say. Tomorrow and the day after tomorrow there is a debate in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> on the health care budget, which Veilig Thuis falls under.

title: IMF also more optimistic about the Dutch economy: growth of 1.5 percent
lead: The Dutch economy continues to perform relatively well, despite economic and political unrest in the world. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has also revised its expectations. For the Netherlands, economic growth of 1.5 percent is expected this year. Earlier the fund had predicted growth of 1 percent. The <entity id="org:centraal-planbureau">Centraal Planbureau</entity> (CPB) had also already revised its expectations. The CPB is counting on economic growth of 1.6 percent this year and 1.4 percent for next year. The IMF thinks the Dutch economy will grow by 1.3 percent next year. The Netherlands seems to be benefiting from the fact that the German economy is doing better again. The IMF expects growth of 1.3 percent in Germany this year, where 0.7 percent was previously expected. Despite Iran war The IMF thinks the global economy will grow 3.1 percent this year and 3.4 percent next year. According to IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, it has succeeded in keeping the effects of the Iran war on oil and gas supplies limited. In addition, growth is being driven by the large amount of investment by big tech companies, she says.

title: A full weapons bin after collection drive in Zaanstreek: 'Mostly the knives shock me'
lead: From knives and punching bags to air rifles and swords: a fair number of weapons were handed in during a collection drive in the Zaanstreek this past week. Residents could hand in their weapons last week anonymously at the police station in Zaandijk, without being punished for possessing prohibited weapons. Especially the knives among them worry the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. The weapons were handed in during a collection action by the municipalities <entity id="org:gemeente-zaanstad">Zaanstad</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-oostzaan">Oostzaan</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-wormerland">Wormerland</entity>, in cooperation with the police. Firearms were excluded from the action, because they could cause dangerous situations in the collection bin. It is the sixth year in a row that people in the Zaanstreek have been able to hand in their weapons. Concerns about stabbing weapons: The weapons bin in the hall of the police station is so full that the lid can barely close. "About a hundred weapons," estimates a police officer when he tips the bin over. After counting, there turn out to be 86. That is slightly more than last year, when a total of 78 weapons were handed in. Among the items handed in are air rifles, batons, airsoft weapons and samurai swords. The police are mainly worried about the smaller knives, punching bags and other stabbing weapons. These are easy to conceal and can cause serious injury. According to the police, such a collection action is urgently needed, especially in the Zaanstreek. "Because there is a lot of violence, especially with knives among young people," says the police officer to the regional broadcaster NH. "We want all of that taken off the streets." He picks up a machete about half a metre long. There are fake blood stains on the sharp blade. "We see this a lot among young people too," he says. "You can imagine that if you get hit with this, it won't end well." Addressing grandchildren: The action is not only about the number of weapons handed in. The police also want to make people aware of the dangers of possessing weapons and to talk with them about it. This became clear, for example, when an elderly woman came to the police station with a bag full of knives. She had addressed her grandchildren about their possession of weapons. She then brought the knives that this produced to the police. "Those are just good actions," the police officer concludes. All handed-in weapons will be destroyed later.

title: Twelve days without trains between Arnhem and Utrecht due to works
lead: From Tuesday 20 to and including Saturday 31 October, no trains will run on parts of the route between Arnhem and Utrecht. During that period ProRail is working on the track and building a new railway underpass at Wolfheze station. The works will take place in two phases. From 20 to and including Friday 23 October, no trains will run between Driebergen-Zeist and Arnhem Centraal and between Driebergen-Zeist and Rhenen. After that, train traffic between Arnhem Centraal and Ede-Wageningen will stop from Saturday 24 to and including 31 October. NS is deploying replacement buses on the routes. Travellers are advised to travel by train wherever possible, as replacement bus services are expected to be very busy. Those travelling to Utrecht are best advised to make a detour via 's-Hertogenbosch. Travellers with Amsterdam or further as their destination are advised to travel via Deventer. NS recommends planning the journey shortly before departure in the app. Kirow rail crane: For placing the underpass at Wolfheze station, ProRail is using special equipment, including the Kirow rail crane. That is the largest rail crane in the Netherlands. Interested people can come and watch the operation; ProRail has set up "rail viewing locations" for this purpose. If the works proceed according to plan, ProRail will place the railway underpass in the night of Saturday 24 to Sunday 25 October. The station square in Wolfheze will also be rebuilt to make it more accessible for people with mobility difficulties.

title: No extra training places for dentists, despite growing shortage
lead: Despite the growing shortage of dentists, no extra training places will be added for students who want to become dentists. That is what a letter to Parliament that education minister <entity id="person:rianne-letschert">Rianne Letschert</entity> is sending to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> today shows. According to the minister, expanding the dentistry programme is "very costly" and would cost 30.1 million euros every year. With this decision the minister is disregarding the advice of the Capaciteitsorgaan, an independent foundation that researches how many dentists and other care professionals will be needed in the future. Last December the advisory body recommended increasing the number of training places to 386 per year. There are currently 270, and from next year 290. 'Training programmes have enough room' Etienne Verheijck, education director of the dentistry faculty Acta in Amsterdam, is disappointed that the minister is not adopting the advice. "We think this is unwise. We had hoped the advice would be followed, at least in part. Yes, it costs money, but the programmes have the room to train more students." The shortage of dentists is expected to keep growing in the coming years. The Capaciteitsorgaan has been advising since 2009 to increase the number of training places. Hans de Vries, chair of the professional organisation of dentists (KNMT), calls it "downright worrying" and "incomprehensible" that the minister is disregarding the advice. In doing so, she would be blocking "a structural solution to keep Dutch oral care accessible in the future". More dental hygienists too Minister Letschert has, however, decided to train more students as dental hygienists. From academic year 2027-2028, 28 additional students may start the higher vocational dental hygiene programme, bringing the total to 381. According to the minister this increase is needed because there will be more "task delegation" from dentists, meaning dental hygienists will take over part of dentists' work. The letter to Parliament does not say what additional costs this will entail. Foreign dentists In the Netherlands the shortage of dentists is increasingly being filled by dentists from abroad. One in four working dentists in the Netherlands is now trained abroad, according to figures from the KNMT. In some regions, such as Zeeland, this already applies to one in two dentists.

title: Ash dieback hits Groningen: '10 percent of the trees will survive this'
lead: Ash dieback is an increasingly big problem in Groningen. The Groningen municipalities keep a close eye on the sick ash trees, but sometimes face difficult choices. Next to a busy road, for example, a sick ash can lead to dangerous situations, and then it may be felled. On the other hand, the municipalities want enough greenery in the area. Ash dieback is caused by a fungus that spreads through the air. The tree then dies off branch by branch. There is currently no cure for the disease. In 2010, ash dieback was first found in Groningen. In the years that followed, the disease spread quickly, partly because many forests in the Netherlands consist only of ash trees. <entity id="org:zbo-staatsbosbeheer">Staatsbosbeheer</entity> estimates that 80 percent of all ash trees in the Netherlands are affected. Of all those trees, 43 percent are in <entity id="org:provincie-flevoland">Flevoland</entity>. Groningen ranks second with 12 percent in terms of ash density. 'Only 10 percent will survive the disease' "That is because of the damp Groningen soil", says tree expert Bert Plaat of the Bomenstichting to RTV Noord. "The ash loves that, that damp, nutrient-rich soil." Plaat first saw ash dieback in 2015. "In the Kuzemerkooi, a small nature area of about 10 hectares near Niekerk. It is full of ash trees, of which about 90 percent are now infected." The Stichting Groninger Bomenwacht, which checks trees in the province for diseases, carried out a study in 2017 into ash dieback among the Groningen municipalities. At that time, most municipalities estimated that the disease rate was above 50. In some cases the percentage was even between 75 and 100. Plaat: "Just assume that ultimately no more than 10 percent of the ash trees will survive the disease." No direct felling When the fungus is found in ash trees, this does not mean they are immediately felled. Initially, the municipalities place the trees under extra supervision. The ash trees are then checked more often. As long as they pose no direct danger, they remain standing. In general, intervention is faster when the trees stand along a busy road. The risk of a sick ash depends not only on the condition of the tree, but also on the location, says the municipality of Groningen, which has 16,000 ash trees. "Trees in heavily visited locations, such as along roads, cycle paths or walking routes, pose a greater risk to the surroundings than trees in a forest planting." The <entity id="org:gemeente-westerkwartier">gemeente Westerkwartier</entity>, where almost 8,000 ash trees stand, has even decided not to intervene at all in forests. "We do this because dead trees are important in a healthy forest. As dead trees decompose, nutrients return to the soil." Clearing and replanting whole forests When trees have to be felled after all, the municipalities in most cases plant new ones in their place. The <entity id="org:gemeente-midden-groningen">gemeente Midden-Groningen</entity>, where just over 3,700 ash trees stand, is carrying out large-scale forest management in various parks and nature areas. There the ash trees are so affected that the municipality has decided to clear entire sections and replant them, this time with different tree species. "In this way we want to make the new planting less vulnerable to diseases, pests and changing climate conditions", the municipality says. A tolerant tree The municipalities cannot say exactly how much money they are spending on combating ash dieback, because the costs fall under general green space management. Tree expert Plaat has sympathy for the ash in any case. "It is a very tolerant tree", he says. "Compare it to a beech, which is very selfish, nothing is allowed to grow under it. But under an ash, everything can grow and it teems with vegetation."

title: Canadian military base hit by 'major incident' with many casualties
Albert Heijn detected hacker traffic, attack via multiple foreign servers
lead: Albert Heijn is dealing with a hacking attack or a serious attempt at one. Officially, the supermarket chain does not want to say what its "cybersecurity incident" exactly involves, but sources in the security world report that Albert Heijn has identified suspicious attack traffic on its systems. It appears that Albert Heijn's ICT security staff saw suspicious traffic coming in and decided to shut down the ICT systems. In doing so, they managed to prevent the hackers from penetrating the systems further. So far, Albert Heijn has spoken of a "cybersecurity incident" in which parts of the system were shut down "as a precaution". Multiple computer servers The company knows of several computer servers that were used in the attack, the sources who wish to remain anonymous report. They concern computer servers in the United States, Poland, Moldova and Turkey. That means the attackers used multiple computer servers in several countries to attack. Which server they use says nothing about their physical location: it is easy to route internet traffic through a server in another country. "Albert Heijn has apparently identified the hackers' infrastructure, which they used to explore the systems or with which they wanted to steal data from the Albert Heijn systems", says computer security expert Pim Takkenberg, who regularly assists hacked companies. Information shared Albert Heijn has shared information about the hackers' infrastructure with other companies so that they can better secure their systems. Companies generally only do this when they have serious indications that a server was involved in an attack. Albert Heijn's investigation shows that servers of Ahold's American division may also be involved. "That could mean the hackers broke into those servers and used them to attack Dutch systems", says Takkenberg. That is not yet certain. Contact the editors The NOS is investigating the hacking attack at Albert Heijn. Do you work at Albert Heijn or do you have other information and want to contact us? That can be done by email or via Signal: @schellevis.86 "We take the cybersecurity incident very seriously", Albert Heijn said in a written response. "In the interest of the investigation and security, we cannot go into technical details or specific security measures at this time." The company does say that no customer data appears to have been stolen. That Albert Heijn has tracked down specific servers says little about whether the attack succeeded, says cybersecurity expert Joey Fennis. "There are hackers involved in any case, but how successful they were cannot yet be said based on this. It is also possible that Albert Heijn detected them in time." Significant consequences Since Sunday afternoon, Albert Heijn has been dealing with the "cyber incident", which has significant consequences both online and offline. The website, apps and customer service of the stores are unreachable due to technical problems, and ordered groceries were not delivered. Several distribution centers are still down. Albert Heijn said at the end of the morning that it was restocking supermarkets again. A source with knowledge of the logistics system tells the NOS that this is going in a rather unstructured way. Ahold reported this afternoon that it is working on a "controlled restart of certain systems".

title: Netherlands not ready for large military transport in case of war, says Court of Audit
lead: Our roads and rail network are not ready for large military transports during a war on our continent, although under NATO agreements we are expected to play a major role in this. That is the conclusion of the Netherlands Court of Audit after research. At least 9.5 billion euros is needed to meet all requirements for the routes, the so-called military corridors. There is already a large shortfall for the maintenance and construction of bridges, roads and rail in our country: 80 billion according to <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>, of which already more than 20 billion by 2038 . An additional financial problem comes on top of that for preparing the military transit routes in our country to, for example, Eastern Europe, says the Court of Audit. The advisor to the cabinet finds it worrying that not enough money is being set aside for this in the coming years. According to Barbara Joziasse of the Court of Audit, "choices will have to be made" by politicians. Strategic location Due to our strategic location on the North Sea, our country is a suitable transit country for European transports in wartime, and agreements have been made about this within NATO. It concerns the transport of equipment such as tanks, smaller vehicles or weapon systems for allies. The Court of Audit notes that some vehicles with "exceptional dimensions" cannot currently use the corridors. Where they can, a large part of the infrastructure is due for renewal and replacement. Joziasse: "Outdated bridges already cause problems for freight traffic. That applies even more so to military equipment". Societal impact Our country is also not well prepared for the consequences of large-scale military transports. If war comes and military equipment is transported on a large scale, this will have a major impact on other traffic. That traffic will partly come to a standstill or have to detour, the Court of Audit outlines, with all consequences "for social life". Problems can also arise on the rail network. Transporting wide equipment may mean that not only one track but also an adjacent track cannot be used. The exact routes of the military corridors are confidential. On Friday the cabinet will announce which bridges and roads will be given priority for maintenance or replacement in the coming period. With the billions needed for the military corridors, even more difficult choices are coming. Nevertheless, it is the aim of the cabinet that in the event of war on our continent "large-scale and long-term military transport takes place as efficiently and unhindered as possible", says <entity id="person:vincent-karremans">minister Karremans</entity> (VVD) of Infrastructure in a response. According to Karremans, part of the information needed to sharpen the estimate of the final costs of the adjustments is still "in motion" in Europe. When there is more clarity on this, Karremans will further inform <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Kamer</entity>.

title: Tomorrow is the first strike day in regional transport, public transport in big cities still runs
lead: Tomorrow is the first strike day in regional transport, as part of a series of strikes that will continue until Christmas. In large parts of the country, no trains or buses will run from regional carriers Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Transdev and Keolis. NS trains will run as normal. Last Friday, the unions FNV and CNV announced that they would strike one day each week because collective labour agreement negotiations had failed. The impact of tomorrow's strike is still unclear. It is up to the employees themselves to decide whether they strike. The carriers have no influence on this. In a number of large cities, transport will at least continue. The carriers in The Hague (HTM) and Amsterdam (GVB) are not taking part in the strike because they provide city transport rather than regional transport. In Rotterdam, the RET trams and metro will run, but the buses will not. In Utrecht, few or no buses and trams are expected to run. Taking to the streets anyway: According to a survey of carriers by news agency ANP, buses and trains are still expected to run, but it will only become clear tomorrow which routes that will be in each region. That depends on how many employees go to work despite the strike. Carriers advise travellers to take cancellations and delays into account. During the national public transport strike at the start of September, it turned out that some bus drivers went to work despite planned strikes. They did not want to leave people who depend on public transport in the lurch. A different day each week: The unions say they understand that the strike is inconvenient for travellers. With the strikes, the unions want wages for employees in the transport sector to rise, staff to get permanent contracts more quickly, and a better early retirement scheme to be introduced. The unions only announce shortly in advance each week which day that week will be a strike day. The intention is for this to be a different day each week, so that carriers cannot prepare with an emergency timetable and travellers are not affected on the same day every week.

title: China imposes sanctions on Paraguay and Belize for supporting Taiwan
lead: China has imposed sanctions on ministers from Paraguay and Belize because these countries maintain diplomatic relations with Taiwan. China regards Taiwan as a breakaway province that must, if necessary by force, be reunited with the People's Republic. Ministers from these countries in Central and South America held meetings with their Taiwanese colleagues last month. According to China, they have spread disinformation and interfered in domestic affairs. All assets they may have in China will be frozen, they may no longer enter the country, and they may not cooperate with Chinese individuals and organisations. The penalties imposed on them are mainly symbolic, because government officials from those countries usually do not travel to China or hold assets there. Last twelve: Paraguay and Belize are among the last twelve countries and governments that recognise Taiwan as an independent state. This means, for example, that they have an embassy on the island. The countries have not yet responded to the sanctions from China. The Netherlands does not officially recognise Taiwan, but does cooperate intensively in the fields of economy, technology, science, agriculture and culture. The Netherlands has no official embassy in Taiwan, but does have an office in the capital Taipei where visa applications and consular affairs are handled. 11 countries and 1 <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> that recognise Taiwan. In recent years China has steadily increased military pressure on Taiwan, almost daily sending fighter jets and warships to fly or sail near the island state. China has also campaigned to win over countries that supported Taiwan. For example, Nauru, Honduras and Nicaragua have shifted their loyalty from Taiwan to China in recent years. US and arms deliveries: The US Department of State has stated that the government of President Trump "opposes coercion and aggression by China against countries in our region that use their sovereign rights". "We stand alongside our friends and partners, including Taiwan, to advance our shared prosperity, security and values," a spokesperson for the ministry said. Although the US does not officially recognise Taiwan, since 1979 it has been an important international pillar of support for Taiwan and regularly supplies weapons to the island so it can defend itself against China. In the first year of this Trump administration, more weapons have already been sold to Taiwan than during the four years under President Biden. Bargaining chip: After a visit by Trump to China in May, there appeared to be a shift in that policy. Shortly afterwards, a planned arms delivery was suspended. Trump also called that arms package "a good bargaining chip" after his visit. It was the first time a US president referred to Taiwan as a trump card rather than an ally. Now concern about growing Chinese influence in the US's South American 'backyard' seems to be gaining the upper hand again. China and Taiwan have been governed separately since 1949. That year the Communist Party came to power in Beijing. The defeated Nationalist Kuomintang fled to Taiwan. The island has had its own government ever since.

title: Van Weel to talk with Halsema about Hamas support at demonstration
lead: <entity id="person:david-van-weel">Minister Van Weel</entity> of Justice will talk with <entity id="person:femke-halsema">burgemeester Halsema</entity> of <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity> about the pro-Palestinian demonstration on Sunday in the capital. People from outside the organisation who came to the protest displayed Hamas flags and expressed support for that Palestinian terrorist organisation. "This went far beyond my limit", Van Weel said this afternoon in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. The BBB had brought him to the question hour to provide an explanation. He finds it terrible that people glorify Hamas three years after the massacre of 7 October in Israel. "Then you are either naive, ill-intentioned or deranged." He thinks the demonstration must have been very intimidating for Jewish residents of Amsterdam. Van Weel therefore wants to talk with mayor Halsema. He wants to know from her why she allowed the demonstration at the National Monument on the Dam to go ahead in this way. Face-covering clothing was worn, and that alone can be a reason to disband a demonstration. She also could have removed the real instigators among the demonstrators. That did happen in <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity>, for example, at an extreme right-wing demonstration on the Malieveld. Van Weel wants to consult with the mayors so that the matter is handled in the same way everywhere in the country. He also called on the House to deal with a bill against the glorification of terror as quickly as possible. According to the minister, that would make many of the banners and expressions from last Sunday prohibited. Just below the line Right-wing parties in the House in particular were not satisfied with Van Weel's answers. "It is all weak, weak, weak", said BBB MP Van der Plas. She wants the minister to take measures right away. In her view, the current law already offers that possibility. "Why is nothing being done about it?" But Van Weel maintains that he really needs the legal amendment to address this. The public prosecution service decides in most cases not to prosecute, because demonstrators "keep staying just below the line" of what is punishable. "They laugh at us", he said. Last Wednesday a similar protest on the Dam, where support for Hamas was also expressed, was disbanded. But that happened because some of the demonstrators did not follow the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>'s instructions about the route. Addressed The organisation of the protest distances itself from the Hamas flags and emphasises that these are people who did not belong to the demonstration. "We as organising groups have repeatedly asked the people with these banners to remove the banners, but they did not want to", says Esther van der Most of Plant een Olijfboom. "Our protest had a diverse programme with both Palestinian and Jewish people on the stage, drawing attention to the ceasefire declared on 10 October 2025, which is not a ceasefire, since the genocide in Gaza continues every day." Red Line On 8 November a Red Line demonstration against the situation in Gaza is planned in Amsterdam. JA21 wanted the assurance that no one from <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> will be present there, because according to MP Nanninga the organisation of the demonstration is linked to Hamas. In the past, <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> walked along at a Red Line event. Van Weel will discuss the issue in <entity id="org:ministerraad">de ministerraad</entity>, but he gave no assurance. The <entity id="org:directoraat-generaal-algemene-inlichtingen-en-veiligheidsdienst">AIVD</entity> states that Hamas has been involved in pro-Palestinian protests in the Netherlands, but according to Van Weel it is not established that this also applies to the Red Line demonstrations. "Of course it is not prohibited in itself to express your support for the Palestinian population. You do have to make that distinction", he said in addition.

title: No place for demonstrators on stadium grounds at AZ match against Israeli club
lead: For fear of confrontations between demonstrators, supporter groups and the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, the <entity id="org:gemeente-alkmaar">gemeente Alkmaar</entity> has designated a demonstration site outside the stadium grounds ahead of the football match between AZ and the Israeli club Hapoel Be'er Sheva. That Europa League match is being played Thursday evening. Two demonstrations have been registered with the municipality in connection with the match.
