It is being investigated whether the officials and hospital staff should be prosecuted. Lead is a toxic heavy metal that accumulates in the human body and can cause serious damage to the brain, the nervous system, the kidneys and the circulatory system. According to the World Health Organization, it is "particularly harmful to young children".

title: Malfunction at electronic passport control at Schiphol resolved
lead: The malfunction at the electronic passport control at Schiphol is over, the Royal Marechaussee reports. A spokesperson says it was an ICT malfunction and not a cyberattack. The gates can be used again and the queues are expected to shorten quickly. The cause of the malfunction is not yet known. It is still being investigated. The malfunction began at 06.00. As a result, all 78 electronic control gates at the airport could not be used. All travellers had to be checked manually. The Marechaussee deployed extra staff so that all counters were staffed. One to one and a half hours of waiting Long queues formed in the arrival and departure halls. Because of the autumn holiday, it was extra busy at Schiphol. According to a spokesperson, people waited an average of one hour, with peaks of one and a half hours. According to KLM, as much as possible was done to wait for passengers. Schiphol says that several hundred people missed their flight due to the malfunction. Transavia earlier said it would be "extra accommodating" with rebooking. Schengen area The electronic passport control can be used by travellers aged 14 and older from the European Union and the Schengen area. People from countries including the United Kingdom, the US and South Korea can also use it. At the so-called eGates, travellers must have their passport scanned and then look straight into the camera.

title: One dead in house fire in Terneuzen, several apartments uninhabitable
lead: A resident died in a fire in an apartment complex in Terneuzen last night. The victim is a 50-year-old man from Terneuzen, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> reports. The fire on the Diepenbrockstraat was reported around 22.30 hours. Emergency services turned out in large numbers. A trauma helicopter was also called in, Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-zeeland">Zeeland</entity> reports. The fire was in an apartment on the second floor. Because of the scale of the fire, all residents of the apartment block had to leave their homes as a precaution. They were taken in at a sports hall. Uninhabitable Around 23.00 hours the fire brigade had the flames under control. A large part of the residents could then return to their homes. That does not apply to everyone, as a number of homes are temporarily uninhabitable. Replacement housing has been arranged for those residents. Mayor Weerwind visited the location last night to encourage the affected residents. Nothing has been made public about the cause of the fire.

title: After half a year of the Iran war, calm has returned to the Gulf states, but certainty has not yet
lead: After months of fighting in the Middle East, a certain calm has returned to the cities on the Persian Gulf. In Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi, schools, restaurants and offices are largely operating as before. Residents still feel safe there. Still, there is uncertainty about the future. Above all, the question of what happens between America and Iran after the American midterm elections of 3 November is keeping the Gulf region busy. In Dubai you would almost forget there was a recent war. The terraces and restaurants are full, there are traffic jams on the motorways, and new migrant workers are settling in the city again. Daily life is also continuing in Doha and Abu Dhabi. The rocket and drone attacks that hit the cities earlier this year have faded into the background. "With all the planned events, such as the World Investment Forum, Formula 1 and the Doha Forum, it seems we are 'back to normal' again," says a Dutch diplomatic source in the region to the NOS. Dark clouds Still, the calm is relative. The war with Iran is not over, but seems to have entered an intermediate phase. President Trump has said he does not intend to attack Iran again before the midterm elections. But what happens after that is uncertain. That recent escalation in Saudi Arabia underlines how fragile the calm is. During Houthi attacks from Yemen on Riyadh airport last week, at least 17 people were killed and more than 300 injured. The airport was closed and air traffic was seriously disrupted. In the article below you can read more about the tensions between both parties: That has turned the tables. Whereas Riyadh was earlier in the war still a refuge for residents of the Gulf states, residents of the Saudi capital are now moving to cities on the Persian Gulf to fly from there. Notably, the public warning system in Riyadh stayed silent for almost two weeks despite repeated attacks. Only on Monday did residents receive an air raid alert on their phones again. According to news agency Reuters, the constant warnings during the first attacks caused irritation, and the authorities feared they would disrupt daily life. Qatar too is taking dark economic clouds into account. Emir Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani warned that everyone, from government to citizens, must be prepared for "the worst conceivable scenarios". His words, together with the recent escalation in Riyadh, illustrate the dilemma of the Gulf states. After all, how do you keep the trust of residents and investors while the threat of new attacks persists? Safety as a selling point The Gulf states have invested billions over the past decades to attract foreign companies, wealthy migrants and tourists. Dubai grew into an international financial centre, Qatar invested in aviation, education and international events, and Saudi Arabia is trying with mega projects to make its economy less dependent on oil. Safety was the key asset in this. While wars raged elsewhere in the Middle East, residents of the Gulf states could count on stability. That image has taken a hit, but has not disappeared. When the first missiles and drones reached the Gulf in February, the shock was great. Meanwhile the sense of safety has returned and daily life is largely going on as usual. But especially among tourists and people outside the region, reluctance remains great. So the war seems to be not only a security problem for the Gulf, but also an image problem. Economic uncertainty For Dutch entrepreneurs in the region, the uncertainty is palpable. Disruptions to air traffic and shipping drive up costs, while tourism in particular is stalling. "Some small entrepreneurs have indeed packed up their things because there is simply no work here for the moment," says a Dutch consultant in Dubai, on condition of anonymity. Larger companies are also becoming more cautious, he notices. "I wouldn't call it panic, but people have become a bit more realistic about the situation here." According to him, concern about the consequences grows if the uncertainty lasts for months. For now normal life goes on and the cities on the Persian Gulf are "open for business". Children go to school, companies organise events and most foreigners see no reason to leave. But behind that normality lies the realisation that the future of the region is strongly influenced by what happens in Washington, Tehran and Tel Aviv.

title: France shocked after protest day with 'unprecedented violence' and 2,000 arrests
lead: "Uprising", "chaos", "the republic in flames", the French press headlines this morning. France wakes up to devastation after a day of large-scale riots. Streets are strewn with glass, fences, tear gas grenades, burned belongings and all kinds of other rubbish. Clean-up crews are trying to make the cities presentable again, shopkeepers are sweeping their own pavements. The total extent of the damage is not yet known, but that it is enormous is clear. On Saturday, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets at at least 110 locations across the country to protest against government policy, the state of education and the rising cost of living. Looting The protests were largely peaceful, but in many cities the demonstrations attracted groups of rioters. In Paris, Marseille, Toulouse, Lille, Angers, Lyon and Bordeaux among others, the protests escalated into riots, vandalism and violence. Cars and bins were set on fire, countless shops were looted, from small supermarkets to upmarket stores. Demonstrators threw fireworks, stones and other objects at the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, which intervened with tear gas and water cannons. Security services in Paris report that there were 1,500 fires in public spaces. Sixty buildings have been on fire. Images of the damage on Sunday morning: According to Minister Nuñez of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, 2,000 people have been arrested. The number of injured emergency workers now stands at 600. According to Nuñez these are still provisional figures. The police are still identifying more perpetrators. In Paris, 111 injured demonstrators have been reported. A demonstrator in Saint-Étienne, in central France, lost a hand to a grenade. 'Only the flag is left' Mayors, shopkeepers, politicians and people on the street are reacting with disbelief and horror to Saturday's riots. People are in shock at the "unprecedented level of violence", or are ashamed of what has happened in their country. In Limoges the last smouldering remains of the town hall are being extinguished this morning. The fire in the historic town hall, set by rioters, is under control, but the building dating from 1883 has largely been lost. The fire brigade rescued the French flag from the building and handed it to the mayor of the city. "This may be the only thing left of the town hall," he said. In daylight the damage to the building is clearly visible: Mayors of various cities are responding sharply to the events. They speak of a "wild horde", "violent groups that are only out for destruction" and "systematic looting". In several places it appeared that the groups were acting very methodically, authorities report. The French judiciary has started an investigation into the degree of organisation behind these groups. The mayors of the three largest cities - Paris, Marseille and Lyon - call what happened in their cities yesterday unacceptable. They want a conversation with Prime Minister Lecornu as soon as possible. Shopkeepers' associations demand financial support from the state. And a request for a parliamentary inquiry committee has also already been submitted. President Macron gives a speech this evening at 8 p.m. Police deployment The police too are reacting dismayed this morning. "We have been through hell," the police union tells Le Parisien. In some places the police seemed totally overwhelmed by the rioters. "Nobody came to help us." He points to the major staff shortage in the police. The deputy mayor of Paris speaks of a lack of resources for the police to stop this kind of scenes. At the same time, voices are also rising that disapprove of the heavy police intervention. "We have the right to fight for decent conditions at school without being hit by a grenade," says the mayor of Marseille this morning. Meanwhile, peaceful demonstrators are also fed up that their protest has been overshadowed by violence. "All those men in black with masks have no placards, they have no demands, and that makes everything we have to say invisible," says a demonstrator to FranceInfo. "I have a placard. One for the environment and also for a fairer distribution of prosperity." Some say to French media that they hope the demonstrations will continue despite the violence. In France, a day after the major riots, the damage is being assessed:

title: Six fugitive suspects arrested for shooting police officer in Belgium
lead: Police teams from several European countries have arrested six men in connection with a shooting earlier this week, in which a Belgian officer lost his life. That is what the Brussels prosecutor reported at a press conference. The suspects all come from Brussels and are known to police for drug cases. One of the suspects is a minor. The six were on the run and were all arrested "in the hours before the press conference", in three different countries, the prosecutor reports. Three men had fled to southern Spain and were arrested there in the city of Almería. They may have been on their way to Morocco. One suspect was arrested at a train station in Paris. Two others were arrested in Belgium. The prosecutor wants to bring the suspects in Spain and France to Belgium as quickly as possible. Shot in the head Last Monday a police officer was killed in Belgium, 41-year-old Nordine El Talbi. The Flemish broadcaster VRT writes that he was a very experienced and valued colleague. After a chase of a stolen car, he was shot in the head in the village of Jette, north of Brussels. El Talbi died not long afterwards in hospital. The stolen car had been forcibly taken from its owner in Tubeke, a place south of Brussels. The police started the chase when traffic cameras flagged the stolen car entering Brussels, De Standaard reported. Drugs and weapons Five of the men now arrested were, according to police, in the stolen car. The car itself was already found in Jette on Monday. Drugs and three weapons were found in the vehicle, the Brussels prosecutor confirms at the press conference.

title: 'Fryslân's oldest communist' and longest-serving councillor Rinze Visser (87) has died
lead: The Frisian politician Rinze Visser has died at the age of 87, the Communist Party of the Netherlands (CPN) reports. Visser was the longest-serving municipal councillor in the Netherlands and at the same time one of the last communist elected representatives. Visser was elected as a councillor for the communist party in the municipality of Lemsterland in 1970, which later merged into <entity id="org:gemeente-de-fryske-marren">De Fryske Marren</entity>. He remained a councillor for more than 55 years, but in March of this year he did not stand for re-election due to his deteriorating health. In the 1970s Visser was also a member of the <entity id="org:provincie-fryslan">Friesland</entity> Provincial Council. Visser grew up in Lemmer. Through his father he came into contact with communist ideals at an early age. At home De Waarheid, the party newspaper of the CPN, was read. At the age of 21 he became a member of the party, writes Omrop Fryslân. "A better world and a better distribution of wealth", was how he described his motivation at the time. "And putting an end to the powerlessness of a large group in the community." Change of course In the 1980s the CPN wanted to merge into a broad progressive movement. Because Visser disagreed with this change of course, he switched in 1985 to the Verbond van Communisten in Nederland (VCN). After various regroupings, Visser returned to the CPN. Because Visser could count on a lot of support in Lemmer and surrounding areas, he was re-elected fourteen times in a row. In the municipal elections of 2022 he ran for the last time as lead candidate for a new four-year term. "The voice we make heard is more relevant than ever. Income differences have never been this large", he said at his fourteenth installation. No successor With Visser's decision not to stand for re-election in the elections this spring, communism disappeared from Frisian politics. The party could not find a successor. "Rinze remained loyal to his ideals and principles throughout his life, also in the difficult years of the counter-revolutions in the socialist countries or when his health made the work difficult", the CPN writes. "Rinze continued to fight steadfastly from the conviction that a better, socialist future is necessary and possible."

title: Albert Heijn delays restart of deliveries again, app and site working again
lead: The problems following the cyberattack at Albert Heijn have still not been resolved, but parts are slowly getting back on track. The app and the site work again, but ordering groceries is still not possible. Albert Heijn now says that deliveries will be restarted on Friday. The supermarket chain says that delivery drivers will then hit the road again "gradually". All orders placed for Friday 23 October will be cancelled. Placing new orders is also still not possible until then. On Thursday the company reported that no groceries would be delivered at least until and including today. A day later this was adjusted and the company expressed the hope that deliveries could start again in "the second half of the week". Now the ordering and delivery problems will therefore last at least until Friday. The customer service also remains unreachable. Loyalty points and stamps: the Albert Heijn app is largely working again, and all saved balances and points have been kept, the supermarket chain reports. Missed purchase stamps can still be obtained on presentation of till receipts. Last Sunday Albert Heijn took its systems offline due to a so-called "cybersecurity incident". According to sources at NOS it was a hacking attack. It quickly led to empty shelves, because distribution was also hit. Since Wednesday the supply to stores has got going again. Who is behind it is still unclear. Albert Heijn says it still cannot make any statements about the incident. There are also reportedly no indications that personal data was involved in the cybersecurity incident.

title: Danish cleaner trapped for more than three days in underground cell
lead: A Danish cleaner was locked in an underground cell for more than three days last month. The Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet reports this. The woman was cleaning in the former Supreme Court building in Copenhagen when a cell door in the basement accidentally slammed shut behind her. These doors cannot be opened from the inside. No phone on her The woman, whose age has not been disclosed, did not have a phone with her and therefore could not call for help, the newspaper writes. Knocking on the door was also pointless, because the building is only used sporadically. The Supreme Court was previously located in the historic building, but a few years ago it moved to another part of the city. The building in the city centre is sometimes still used today by the Copenhagen District Court. The building is near Amalienborg Palace, where Danish King Frederik lives with his wife Mary and their four children. The world-famous statue of the Little Mermaid is also within walking distance. Man alerts police The incident with the cleaner happened just over a month ago, on Wednesday 16 September at 18.00. The woman's husband had been away for a few days and discovered upon returning home that she was missing. He then began a search and found her bicycle at the historic building in the city centre. He then alerted the police. After her release, the woman was taken to hospital. After the incident, all cell doors were checked and the locks replaced, the newspaper writes. From now on, cell doors can only be locked from the outside. The cleaning company the woman works for says the employee has received psychological support. "The employee is doing well under the circumstances and has returned to work at their own request", the company wrote in a response to the newspaper. Belgian politician stuck on toilet for thirteen hours The story of the Danish woman recalls an incident in Belgium that happened at about the same time. Belgian politician Frédéric Erens was stuck on the toilet for thirteen hours last month because the lock turned out to be jammed. He also did not have his phone with him. Erens could not sleep because, in his view, the space was too small. Early in the morning, the man was discovered by a cleaner. "There is no point in getting annoyed. It could have happened to anyone."

title: Everyone who fell ill after visiting Grolsch brewery is home again
lead: Eleven people who fell ill yesterday after a tour of the Grolsch brewery in Enschede are home again after a check by emergency workers. One of them spent a night in hospital, the brewer tells the NOS. The visitors and two employees had drunk brewing water that is used to brew beer. "Someone said: that tastes strange", says a spokesperson for Grolsch. According to RTV Oost, the water may have contained caustic soda, a corrosive substance that can cause burns. The police are still investigating. According to a police spokesperson, it may have been an accident. "Or something else may be going on." Grolsch makes no statements about possible causes, because the investigation is still ongoing. 'Separate from beer production' According to Grolsch, consumers need not worry about the quality of the beer. "This is separate from beer production and beer products", says the spokesperson. According to the brewery, the tap from which those present drank is separate from the rest of the production process. "The quality and safety are not and have never been at issue." Yesterday several ambulances rushed to the Enschede brewery. A German trauma team was also called in, but in the end this proved not to be necessary.

title: Ten civilians killed in Ukraine, which itself carries out a major drone attack on Russia
lead: Russian attacks on Ukraine have claimed ten civilian lives in one day, according to the newspaper The Kyiv Independent, citing local authorities. At the same time, the Ukrainian army carried out one of its largest drone attacks on Russia since the start of the war last night. In the Russian city of Saint Petersburg, an oil terminal and a data center were among the targets hit. The governor of the city speaks of one dead and five injured. The fire at the oil terminal sent a large plume of smoke hanging over the city, as seen in photos by press photographers. The Russian army claims it shot down 1,256 Ukrainian drones and seven cruise missiles across the country in one day. It is exceptional for Ukraine to have deployed so many drones in one night. Apologies over drones that went astray. It appears that a number of Ukrainian drones also ended up in Polish and Lithuanian airspace during the major attack. In Lithuania an air alarm sounded, and the Polish armed forces also took action after reports of unidentified objects in the airspace. The Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has offered apologies for this. Ukrainian drones were probably knocked off course by Russian jammers, a spokesperson said on social media. Dozens injured in Ukraine. Within 24 hours various Ukrainian regions came under fire from the Russian invasion force. In the eastern oblast of Donetsk, seven deaths and fourteen injuries were reported. Several houses were hit, according to local authorities. Two civilians died in the northeastern region of Sumy, the local government said. In the southern city of Zaporizhzhia one civilian death was reported. Dozens of people were injured across the country. Russia reportedly bombed critical infrastructure again. The Ukrainian army states that 152 Russian drones were neutralised. That number includes sixteen of the hard-to-intercept jet-propelled drones. According to information from the Ukrainian armed forces, ten of these drones got past the air defense systems. The Kremlin claims that logistics centers where drone parts were stored were attacked. The army also says a ship was hit in the southern port city of Odesa. It is claimed that this ship had a military cargo. Logistics centers targeted. In Saint Petersburg, among other things, a logistics center of a Russian online retailer was attacked, and a data center of tech giant VKontakte. The two companies have confirmed that they were hit. Ukraine has long been bombing warehouses of Russian online retailers, such as Wildberries. Recently, data centers have also been attacked. President Zelensky wrongly claimed that in this way "less hate" could be spread by pro-Russian online trolls. Zelensky thanks the US for resuming intelligence sharing. Zelensky said today that Washington is again sharing crucial military intelligence with Kyiv. With this information, warnings can be issued, for example, for Russian missile attacks on Ukrainian cities. "We are very grateful for this," he told NBC News. Earlier this week Zelensky accused the American government of deliberately cutting off the intelligence. American President Trump then claimed that the exchange of this information had never been stopped. Relations between the two presidents have recently cooled considerably again.

title: After lots of sun and high temperatures, autumn seems to be getting going next week
lead: Real autumn has not yet arrived, with lots of sun and relatively high temperatures. Over the coming week, depressions gradually move closer. That brings more wind and unsettled weather. But that is not yet the case on Monday and Tuesday. Those are two dry days. Monday starts with cloud banks, and gradually the sun breaks through more. On Tuesday the sun gets more room in any case. Both days are further characterised by a moderate easterly wind. Monday will be about 15 degrees and Tuesday 12. Unsettled. From Wednesday the depression train gets going. It brings very unsettled weather, with one moment of the day being distinctly autumnal with rain and wind, and a few hours later it can clear up strongly again. The timing of these low-pressure systems always remains somewhat uncertain, so for a part of the day it can sometimes be considerably better or worse. At the moment the wettest days look to be Friday and Sunday, with a chance of lots of wind especially on Friday. In short: autumn seems to be really getting going.

title: Priest in Ecuador dies during mass when a crucifix falls on him
lead: In Ecuador, a Catholic priest died yesterday afternoon after the crucifix fell squarely on him during mass. The archdiocese of the city of Guayaquil has confirmed his death. The mass was broadcast live on social media. The footage shows priest Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari standing behind the altar when the wooden crucifix of the Perpetuo Socorro church suddenly falls from the wall. Then someone calls out: "Father, father... call an ambulance!" It is not clear how many people were present in the church during the incident. The emergency services that rushed to the scene could not save his life. Local media write that the fatal accident has caused enormous shock within the Christian community of Ecuador. In an obituary, the archdiocese writes that it "joins in prayer for the eternal rest of his soul". Sánchez Molinari was also parish priest of the church, meaning he was in charge of the parish.

title: Trump's new voting law was already tested in Kansas in 2014 and it turned into chaos
lead: The American president Trump wants voters to present proof of citizenship and their passport before they may cast their vote in the midterm congressional elections at the start of November. In the state of Kansas this was already tried. It was a dismal failure, and tens of thousands of eligible voters fell victim to it. When Steven Fish from Ottawa, Kansas, wanted to register as a voter in 2014, he had to show his birth certificate. He had no idea where to look for it. The document could be with his stepfather, but he had fallen out with him. And where should he request the original? The military base where he was born had already closed in the 1990s. It may sound strange to the Dutch, but many Americans do not have their birth certificate on hand. Even more: half do not even have a passport. In Kansas there are even fewer. Voters who did have their documents in order also ran into problems. "Women also had to show a marriage certificate to explain why their name differed from the one on their birth certificate," recalls Micah Kubic of civil rights organisation American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). The ACLU stands up for fundamental rights and civil liberties. Tad Stricker did have all the required documents when he applied for a driver's license in Kansas City, and was immediately registered as a voter. But nobody asked for them. When he reported to the polling station, it turned out he was not on the electoral roll. He was allowed to fill in a provisional ballot, but it was not counted: his vote was lost. Fish and Stricker were not the only ones affected by the rule: research showed that the registration of 30.000 residents of Kansas had been wrongly blocked. And the remedy proved worse than the disease: only a few dozen non-citizens had registered, often through misunderstandings. A handful of them had actually cast a vote. "It was certainly not worth losing tens of thousands of votes for that," says Kubic of the ACLU. The figures match the national picture. Even the conservative think tank Heritage Foundation found, over a quarter century and more than a billion votes cast, no more than ninety examples. "The consequence for such fraud is prison or deportation, and almost nobody takes that risk," says Lana Nott of the Campaign Legal Center in Washington D.C. So it usually does not seem to be malicious intent. For example, a mayor in Kansas voted for Trump several times while not being a citizen. Joe Ceballos is of Mexican descent and, as a permanent resident of the US, does have a 'green card'. He says he was not aware that he was not allowed to vote. Ceballos resigned as mayor and was sentenced to a year of suspended imprisonment and a fine. Shortly afterwards he was nonetheless arrested by the immigration service ICE. He has since been released on bail, pending his hearing. Republicans, however, point to a recent scandal in the Democratic state of New Jersey. There, due to a software error, 6600 residents were wrongly registered as eligible to vote. 400 of them actually cast their vote as well. Two million dollars to repay: Steven Fish and Tad Stricker therefore could not cast their votes after all. With the help of the ACLU they sued the state of Kansas. With success: in 2018 the judge declared the rules unconstitutional. Kansas had to repay the plaintiffs almost two million dollars in legal costs. The state appealed, but the higher courts also reached the same conclusion. That meant the end of the 'SAFE Act', as the law in Kansas was called. But through President Trump the law is getting a new life, under an almost identical name: the SAVE Act. Trump is trying to get it through Congress with all his weight, after his presidential decree with similar requirements had run aground in court. This spring Trump even refused to sign other legislation as long as his own party did not rally behind the SAVE Act. Still, there is so far no majority for it in <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity>, although a dozen Republican states have already introduced similar rules. In half of those states the rules already take effect at the upcoming midterms. For Steven Fish it feels like déjà vu. "It is shocking that our voting rights are being undermined again, with the same rhetoric." For Tad Stricker too it feels like a repeat of the same moves. "We have seen this film, and its ending, already," he says. According to Stricker, voters are being deprived of the right to vote for political motives. He fears it will become harder, especially for immigrant Americans, to register as voters. "If I, as a middle-aged white man, am already a victim, how will it turn out for naturalised immigrants?" But even if the rules are not introduced, Trump can use this politically. If Republicans suffer defeat, he can again claim there was election fraud.

title: Macron lashes out at rioters in TV speech as riots continue in Paris
lead: One day after the demonstrations that completely got out of hand in Paris and other French cities, French President Macron lashed out at the rioters in a televised speech. He said that those who caused damage "must pay". "We will not compromise", he added. He also said he wants the damage caused to be recovered from the perpetrators of violence. "Whoever caused damage must pay. Whoever looted must compensate the damage", he said. He explicitly pointed to far-left groups in the country. "Whoever wanted to bring down the Republic will be held accountable." Macron clearly distinguished between the demonstrators who protested peacefully yesterday, and the looters and arsonists. "We must never confuse demonstrators with legitimate demands with those who caused damage. Their voice must be heard without prejudice and without trivialising the problems." 'Firmly uphold order' He further called the violence "unbridled" and "not justifiable". Besides in Paris, yesterday, after weeks of pupil protests, people also took to the streets in at least 110 other places in the country to protest government policy, the state of education and rising costs of living. In many places this went orderly and calmly, also in Paris, but where it went wrong, it also went badly wrong. In Limoges the 19th-century town hall was set on fire, after which the tower collapsed. In Marseille the bust of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic, was destroyed in the town hall. Also, many cars and buildings were set on fire across the country and there was widespread looting. According to the French Ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> 2397 people have been arrested. In his TV speech Macron said he understood the demonstrators' problems. "Our responsibility is therefore twofold: listen to the anger and address its causes, and firmly uphold republican order." However, he did not announce concrete measures to curb the ever-rising cost of living in France. Excerpt from Macron's TV speech: He did point to the conflict in the Middle East as the main cause of price increases in French supermarkets and at the pump. Tomorrow his three-day tour of the Gulf states begins, he then emphasised. He promised the French people that he is continuing his efforts to secure France's fuel and gas supply. Finally, he called on all political parties and social organisations to unequivocally condemn all violence. "The country needs order and reconciliation, not escalation." It remains to be seen whether that will happen. Centre-right presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau finds Macron's speech "very disturbing", he writes on X. According to him, Macron should have declared a state of emergency to "protect the French people". Paris senator Yannick Jadot calls the performance a "terrible demonstration of powerlessness". "Our country is like a drunken ship without a captain taking water from all sides." Unrest again in Paris While Macron addressed the rioters, it was again restless in the streets of Paris. As early as the afternoon, the public order police had to intervene at Place de la République. They deployed tear gas to disperse dozens of masked participants in a demonstration not registered with the city council. A message had circulated on social media calling to "continue the movement". Several French media reported that it then quickly got out of hand again. In the centre of the French capital shops were looted, and many large fires were set. Footage shows dozens of young people destroying the stone fountain around the Monument to the Republic and then throwing debris at the police. After the Paris police, as yesterday, deployed the CRS 8, an elite unit of the French police specifically trained in combating urban violence, the rioters spread into surrounding streets. Especially on the busy Faubourg du Temple street, which runs from Place de la République to the northeast of the city, it got out of hand between youths who tried to make themselves unrecognisable with hoods and the law enforcement services. French newspaper Le Monde reports that rubbish bins are still being set on fire and the rioters are using electric bicycles to build burning barricades. Shops close Also the paper writes that at the start of the evening youths entered a tobacco shop and looted it. Yesterday this shop was also a victim. The owner was in her shop at the time to protect it against the rioters. Eventually she had to be taken to hospital with a head wound. The district mayor of central Paris calls on X for shopkeepers to close their shops. He speaks of vandalism and arson that have flared up again.

title: US threatens 'devastating' countermeasures if Europe does not give SpaceX free rein
lead: European companies face "devastating" countermeasures if Brussels goes ahead with plans to restrict access to the European market for, for example, the American tech company SpaceX of Elon Musk. That is what the American ambassador to the European Union, Andrew Puzder, tells the British newspaper Financial Times. He does not say what those countermeasures would entail. Last summer the European Commission submitted a proposal to reserve part of the frequencies for mobile satellite services exclusively for European companies. For non-European companies, fewer frequencies would consequently remain. The proposal is meant to strengthen Europe's technological sovereignty. It is mainly important to become less dependent on technology from the US, is the message from Brussels, because of the unpredictability of American President Trump. Satellite support in Ukraine Earlier, technology and space company SpaceX already expressed sharp criticism of the European plans. SpaceX states that Europe is endangering satellite support in Ukraine if the frequencies for the company are restricted. Ukrainian soldiers use the military branch of the Starlink satellite network of parent company SpaceX to communicate and control drones in the war against Russia. In recent days the Ukrainian army has had problems with Starlink. According to sources of the news agency Reuters, the White House instructed SpaceX to set limits on the speed of drones. As a result, they could reach a maximum of 160 kilometres per hour instead of top speeds of up to 500 kilometres per hour.

title: 19 more people in critical condition after fatal fire at military base in Canada
lead: 19 of the 39 people who were injured and taken to hospital in the fire at a military base in Canada on Saturday are in critical condition. That is what the premier of the province of Alberta announced. The fire in Wainwright in Alberta killed four soldiers. The incident happened when live ammunition was fired on the military grounds during an exercise. A gas pipeline or gas well may have been hit, after which an explosion followed and the fire broke out. How exactly this could have happened is still being investigated. According to the army there are no indications of a terrorist act. Fire spread quickly. A senior general says that shortly after the fire broke out, it was assumed the fire was under control, when the wind suddenly shifted. The fire then moved rapidly toward places where soldiers were training. According to the general, "the fire was one kilometre away when the wind turned, after which the fire moved one kilometre within 36 seconds". It was not known before the exercise began that it would blow so hard. In the province, gusts of up to 100 kilometres per hour were measured on Saturday. In the province, "code orange" was declared because of the fire, after which emergency services turned out with, among others, 22 ambulances, six aircraft and two helicopters. The victims have been taken to four hospitals in the region. The four soldiers who died have been identified and their families have been informed. Some of the injured have suffered serious burns and may need weeks to months of rehabilitation, says the premier of Alberta. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks of "one of the greatest tragedies for the Canadian army on its own soil in peacetime". He has ordered that flags on government buildings be flown at half-mast.

title: Flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna makes precautionary landing in Bulgaria after bomb threat
lead: A flight that was en route from the Israeli city of Tel Aviv to Vienna in Austria was diverted last evening to Sofia airport in Bulgaria after a bomb threat was made. Bulgarian authorities report this. The Austrian airline Austrian Airlines, which operated the flight, reports this morning that no explosive was found on board. The Austrian Airlines flight had departed from Israel at 18:40 local time and landed in Sofia at 21:42 local time. This happened after the crew reported a "bomb threat signal" at the Romanian border, the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport says. Fighter jet deployed: as is customary according to the ministry, a fighter jet was then deployed to escort the passenger plane to the Bulgarian airport. Once there, the passengers were disembarked and rebooked onto another flight. Austrian Airlines tells Sky News that "we can confirm that a threat was made against the Tel Aviv to Vienna flight, which made a stopover in Sofia necessary". There were 51 passengers and six crew members on board. According to the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, the bomb threat was made by an Austrian citizen who was not on board the flight. Flydubai flight: last month, an aircraft en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv made a dive and landed at an airport in Saudi Arabia. This happened after the co-pilot of the Flydubai flight stabbed the captain. A struggle ensued. Eventually the co-pilot was overpowered by passengers on board. According to the public prosecutor of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the co-pilot, a man from Oman, intended to crash the aircraft, carrying mainly Israelis, at Tel Aviv airport.

title: Wake-up call 19/10: Canadian province of Alberta votes on possible secession • French ministers meet after riots
lead: Good morning! In the Canadian province of Alberta a referendum is being held on a possible secession, and in France the ministers are meeting in a crisis session to discuss the riots of last weekend. First, the weather: cloudy this morning, with mist in the south. Later more sun. It will be 13 to 16 degrees. Are you going out today? Here you can find the overview of traffic jams and roadworks, and here everything about the situation on the rail network. What can you expect today? What did you miss? It was also restless last night in Paris. In the early morning, young people were again arrested for looting shops. This weekend nearly 2,400 people have already been arrested in connection with riots at protests in several cities. Last night, garbage bins and electric bicycles were set on fire. In addition, young people threw pieces of a vandalised fountain at police officers. The demonstrations were mainly aimed at rising prices in France and the state of education. During the course of the day they turned into riots. President Macron says that the perpetrators of the vandalism and violence will pay for it. Other news from the night: And then just this: Yesterday, a day after the demonstrations that completely got out of hand in Paris and other French cities, French President Macron used a televised address to lash out at the rioters. He said that those who caused the vandalism "must pay". He also called for calm. Meanwhile the riots in Paris simply continued. Have a nice day!

title: More than three hundred new arrests for looting in Paris
lead: In Paris yesterday and overnight another 351 people were arrested. The French police report this. According to the police, the group consists of young people who tried to vandalise and loot shops. According to the French news site 20minutes, demonstrators also threw glass bottles at officers. The entrance of an iconic department store was smashed in and forced open, after which looters entered the building. Riots across France There were protests and riots throughout France all weekend. On Saturday hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets at at least 110 locations in the country to protest against government policy, the state of education and rising costs of living. The protests were for the most part peaceful, but in many cities the demonstrations also attracted rioters. In Paris, Marseille, Toulouse, Lille, Angers, Lyon and Bordeaux among others, the protests escalated into riots, vandalism and violence. According to Minister Nuñez of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, at least 2000 people were arrested. At least 600 emergency workers were injured. One person also died of a heart attack. Minister stays Minister Nuñez, whose resignation is being demanded by the left, submitted his resignation to Macron yesterday. The French president acknowledged "shortcomings in preparation and intelligence", but refused to accept the resignation of his Minister of the Interior. Macron says it is necessary that the police and security services have a leader in these times. Last night he gave a speech in which he lashed out at the rioters: Nuñez is expected in Marseille today. The southern French city has been hard hit by the violence; thousands of looters were out there this weekend. Rioters broke into the city hall and attacked the police.

title: Israeli police arrest suspects for attacks in West Bank
lead: Israeli police have arrested ten suspects in the investigation into the attacks in the occupied West Bank over the past weekend. Palestinians, an American photojournalist and European diplomats were attacked. On Friday, Palestinians were attacked by masked settlers during the annual harvest in an olive grove in the West Bank. Photojournalist Heidi Levine of The Washington Post was reporting on the harvest and was assaulted by the group of settlers while wearing a vest with the inscription "PRESS". Her phone, passport and camera were also stolen. Settler violence in the occupied West Bank increases every year around this period due to the olive harvest season. For many Palestinians the olive harvest is a main source of income, but it should also be a festive tradition in which families go out to the land together to pick the olives. Images of Friday's attack: To support Palestinian residents with the olive harvest, European diplomats were in the West Bank a day later. During their visit the convoy was surrounded by masked settlers armed with sticks. A French mayor was injured in this. Belgian and Polish diplomats and representatives of the Roman Catholic Church were also assaulted. 'Stain on society' Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu said about the attack on the Palestinians and the American photojournalist Levine that no premature conclusions should be drawn. Levine said that she is "shocked and offended" by the prime minister's reaction. She said that "Jewish terrorists" were behind the attacks. "I have been covering this region for more than forty years and have never seen this country in such a state as now." The journalist was taken to hospital after the attack. There she received a phone call from Israeli President Herzog. He was "actually very nice", she said. "He is ashamed of what happened. 'These people are a stain on Israeli society', he said." Little prosecution The speed with which the arrests of the ten settlers were made probably has to do with the great international pressure on Israel. US Secretary of State Rubio has asked Israel to act firmly, and the European Union has also strongly condemned the violence. The arrests do not automatically mean that these suspects will also be prosecuted. According to figures from the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din, about 94 percent of the investigations followed by the organisation between 2005 and 2025 ended without an indictment. In 3 percent of cases there was a partial or full conviction. Occupied territory The West Bank, including East Jerusalem, has been occupied by Israel since 1967. More than 700,000 settlers and more than 3 million Palestinians live there. Violence by settlers has increased recently. In July Human Rights Watch reported that attacks in the region more often lead to forced expulsion of Palestinians.

title: Lula and Bolsonaro attack each other in fierce and personal TV debate
lead: A corrupt president who hands his country over to narco-terrorists or a militiaman who sells out Brazilian interests to the US. Accusations flew back and forth in the first televised debate ahead of Sunday's election between President Lula (80) of Brazil and his challenger Flávio Bolsonaro (45). The two are locked in a neck-and-neck race for the favour of Brazilian voters. Bolsonaro narrowly won the first round of the election earlier this month, a surprise, and he is also slightly ahead in the polls now. Both men therefore had a lot at stake, and the debate quickly became fierce and personal. "Lula, under you crime has increased enormously. How do you explain that 73 percent of prisoners voted for you?" Bolsonaro asked the president. He responded with a reference to Bolsonaro's father Jair, who has been sentenced to 27 years in prison for an attempted coup and is now under house arrest: "If only it had been 100 percent, including your father. Then he would have voted for the better man". Economy and security Because of the mudslinging, the policy plans of both candidates moved somewhat into the background during the two hours they spoke. Lula said that on two occasions he had managed to turn around a faltering economy inherited from his predecessors. "I know what is needed to make this country grow", he promised. "They want to privatise 95 percent of all Brazilian state companies, I want strong, productive companies in government hands." Bolsonaro said he wanted to tackle crime more strictly. "If you live in a favela now, in a poor neighbourhood, how much would you like to live without that oppression?" he asked. "I take public safety seriously, because it should be the criminals who are afraid to walk the streets." Bolsonaro also attacked the president over the high cost of living. "Is food more expensive or cheaper? When did you last have a piece of meat in your fridge?" 'Interests sold out' Lula in turn tried to portray Bolsonaro as an American puppet who hands his country over to Trump, who was previously a close ally of his father Jair when he was president. "The Brazilian people certainly know that the Bolsonaros bow to American interests. That is obvious." Bolsonaro countered that under Lula criminal gangs are in charge and that US support is therefore appreciated. He promised to declare drug gangs narco-terrorists and to build half a million additional prison cells. Accusations of liar and thief flew back and forth. The loose format of the debate fuelled the confrontations. The moderators took a restrained approach and the candidates were free to move around the stage, which regularly led to direct confrontations. "Not so close", Lula warned Bolsonaro irritably when he came too close to him. "Calm down, I am not aggressive", he responded. "I want some distance, with all those militiamen in the Bolsonaro family", Lula continued reproachfully, to which Bolsonaro snapped at the president: "Luckily I left my wallet at home, so you cannot rob me". To give his corruption accusations extra impact, Bolsonaro even twisted the word, corruPTo, framing the PT of Lula's party in it. After a corruption conviction by a biased judge, Lula spent nearly a year and a half in prison before the verdict was overturned . Lula proposed that they both give full transparency about their finances and phone records together, "so that the Brazilian people can see who the thieves are in this country". Bolsonaro responded that he had nothing to hide, but did not go further into his opponent's proposal. On Friday there will be a second debate between the two men, two days before Brazil goes to the polls on Sunday.

title: 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza no longer receive emergency aid from the World Food Programme
lead: The World Food Programme (WFP) of the United Nations reports that it must drastically reduce support to Palestinians in Gaza due to funding problems. As a result, half a million Palestinians in the Gaza Strip will be left without monthly food aid. The cuts are taking effect while a large majority of the Palestinian population faces acute food insecurity or worse, the WFP says. Winter is also approaching. "These cuts are happening just as we face the fourth winter," says Carl Skau, deputy director of the WFP. "I have experienced the winters here. They are truly merciless." Cuts The cuts in the Gaza Strip come as no surprise. This year the WFP was already forced, due to shortages, to allocate less money for emergency aid in Gaza, and last month emergency aid to Palestinians in the occupied West Bank was also scaled back. There, 400,000 Palestinians previously received aid; now that has been reduced to 200,000. The aid programme announced last month that further cuts in Gaza would be "unavoidable" without extra money. The World Food Programme receives money from governments and private donors, but it has seen that income decline in recent years. The United States is the largest donor, but under President Trump its support has fallen sharply. For the coming six months, some 450 million dollars (just over 400 million euros) would be needed for essential work in the Palestinian territories. Warm meals Since the ceasefire in October 2025, the World Food Programme has provided food and financial aid to 1.6 million Palestinians in Gaza. The humanitarian organisation distributes, among other things, food parcels, hot meals, bread and snacks for children at school. But the WFP says it "no longer has sufficient resources" to continue this support. This means that since this month, 1.1 million people still receive aid from the organisation, roughly half the population of the area. As a result, half a million Palestinians no longer receive emergency aid, 100,000 fewer hot meals are distributed daily, and families in hard-to-reach areas will now receive a hot meal every other day instead of daily. The number of food parcels families receive has also been reduced from two to one, and families will receive a smaller bag of wheat flour. In addition, 75,000 families receive less financial support. Dependent on food aid In the densely populated Gaza Strip, Israeli attacks in recent years have led to large-scale destruction. A large part of the Palestinian population has been displaced and depends on food aid. After the Hamas terror attack of 7 October 2023, Israel began a devastating war in Gaza. Earlier this year Israel confirmed that roughly 71,000 Palestinians have been killed in it. In reality the death toll is much higher. For example, missing persons are not included in the figures, while an estimated ten thousand Palestinians are missing. Israel also only counts people who were killed as a direct result of Israeli attacks. Despite the fragile ceasefire in Gaza, which has now been in force for just over a year, Israel continues to carry out attacks. Aid organisations said in June that the situation in Gaza is still dire and dangerous, and that there is a shortage of almost everything. WFP deputy director Skau agrees. "Life here is still very cruel." According to Skau, basic facilities are lacking and it is not safe.

title: Disappearance of Amelia Earhart remains a mystery after 89 years: 'Plane wreck' turns out to be tree trunks
lead: An international group of researchers has failed to solve the disappearance of Amelia Earhart in the 1930s. A mysterious object spotted in 2020 on aerial photos of an atoll in the Pacific Ocean turns out not to be a plane wreck but a pile of tree trunks. An atoll is a ring-shaped or horseshoe-shaped island. "It has been a mystery for 90 years and it will remain a mystery for now," says expedition leader Rick Pettigrew in an update from Nikumaroro. "The island had secrets and still does not reveal them." The 39-year-old Earhart disappeared with her navigator Fred Noonan when she tried to become the first woman to fly around the world. After they departed from Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937, they vanished during the crossing towards Hawaii. A massive search turned up nothing, and it remains one of the best-known disappearances in aviation. The Purdue University in the American city of Indianapolis, which had financed Earhart's plane at the time, now organised an expedition to find out whether her aircraft may have ended up on the remote atoll of Nikumaroro. Aerial photos showed a formation off the coast that looked like wreckage. A research team of seventeen people flew to Kiribati at the beginning of this month to make a five-day boat trip from there to Nikumaroro. Somewhat delayed by heavy weather, the team was ultimately able to conduct four days of research on the island. It soon became clear there was no wreck at all. On site it turned out to be a pile of tree trunks, which the current had also largely pulled apart again. The object appeared to glint metallically in photos because, according to the researchers, a hardened layer of coral sand had settled on the wood. Pettigrew does not want to call the expedition a disappointment. "The team is cheerful and proud of what we have achieved," he says in his first reaction. "We have achieved our goal: finding out what this object actually was." He remains convinced that Nikumaroro and Amelia Earhart are connected. An analysis from 2018 of bones found there in 1940 showed they could be those of a woman of Earhart's build. In addition, a woman's shoe and make-up items from the 1930s were once found. "I think someone will eventually find definitive evidence and the mystery will finally be solved." Purdue has already announced that it will continue the search. "The adventure is worth it in itself," expedition member Steve Schultz is quoted as saying about Earhart from the island. "This object may not have been what we hoped it was, but we have done more research, the world has learned more about Nikumaroro, and we have added a new chapter to this story of exploration and discovery."

title: Elderly man falls into 3-metre-deep gap of street container in Den Bosch
lead: A man fell into a 3-metre-deep hole in the street in Den Bosch this morning. Normally an underground container stands at that spot, but it was being emptied at the time, reports Omroep Brabant. The man is said to be an elderly man who lives in a neighbouring care complex. He fell into the hole around 08.00 and reportedly lay there for well over half an hour. He was then taken to the hospital in Tilburg with injuries, the broadcaster reports. A trauma helicopter was called. The area around the underground waste containers has been cordoned off with tape.

title: Australian parliamentarian seriously injured in collision, possibly deliberate
lead: In Australia, a parliamentarian was seriously injured when a car drove into her. The authorities, including Prime Minister Albanese, are considering a deliberate act. The 65-year-old Helen Haines, an independent parliamentarian for a district in the state of Victoria, was unloading her car boot at her party office in the city of Wangaratta when someone drove into her. She reportedly became trapped between the two cars and sustained serious injuries. A bystander managed to get the driver out of the car and restrain him until police arrived. The scene of the incident has been cordoned off by police for investigation. U-turn Prime Minister Albanese speaks of an attack on Haines. Witnesses say the driver deliberately drove into Haines, that he made a U-turn when he passed her and then intentionally hit her. Albanese says nothing is yet known about the motive of the suspect, a 43-year-old man from nearby Tarrawingee. Police also found a knife in his car, but it is unclear whether that has anything to do with the collision. Haines's family says they are grateful for the quick help from bystanders, care providers and police. They do not wish to make any further statements about how Haines is doing and ask that her privacy be respected. 'Decent person' Haines was elected in 2019 as representative for the Indi district, about 250 kilometres northeast of Melbourne. Before that she was a nurse and midwife. Albanese praises her as a skilled colleague. "She is exceptionally intelligent and, even better, a genuinely decent person, full of integrity and respected by the whole parliament", he said. "Our thoughts go out to Helen, her friends, team and community in this difficult time." The prime minister further noted that political discourse in Australia and worldwide has recently become heated, and that politicians are increasingly facing threats. He therefore called for more calm in political discussions. He could not yet say whether there were specific security risks for Haines.

title: Less public transport again on Thursday due to regional transport strike
lead: Employees in regional transport are once again laying down their work on Thursday. As a result, many fewer buses and regional trains will run on 22 October. Last week, regional transport staff also went on strike. The union demands a better collective labour agreement (cao). In addition to a wage increase, the regional public transport workers want, among other things, to know their work schedules well in advance. Input "The employers are still listening insufficiently," says Marijn van der Gaag, director of FNV Streekvervoer. "We will not be fobbed off with a cao that makes work and life outside work worse." The unions want better conditions for older employees. They demand more say in their schedules. They also want to keep allowances for unfavourable hours. The negotiations for a new cao between the employers and the employees are stuck. It concerns some 13,500 employees in regional transport. On Thursday, the national train service and public transport in the big cities will continue as normal.

title: 'Vote for my friend's daughter': Criminals hack your WhatsApp with new trick
lead: Maybe you've even had one yourself: a WhatsApp message from an acquaintance asking you to vote for their daughter in a free dance class. It seems harmless, but whoever clicks the link runs the risk of losing control of their WhatsApp account. This is how it works: after clicking the link, you land on a website where you can cast your vote. To confirm your vote, you have to enter your phone number. Then you are shown a code that you must enter. You think you are confirming your vote, but in reality you are giving criminals access to your WhatsApp account. This method is called GhostPairing (ghost pairing). Criminals abuse the option of using WhatsApp on multiple devices, for example on a laptop. With the code, they link their own device to your account. This way they can read your messages without you noticing and send messages in your name to friends and family. How do you check whether someone is in your WhatsApp? Sophie ter Schure (40) is a victim of the new scam method. "I was asked by an acquaintance to vote and I thought: sure, I send things like that too. The site said only five more votes were needed, so it was done in a moment." After entering her phone number and the verification code, things went wrong. The hackers sent the message in her name on to all her contacts. "I got messages all saying 'You've been hacked!'. I probably got a hundred. My phone exploded." She also got reactions from people who had clicked the forwarded link. "Like: 'done, thanks'", says Ter Schure, who feels guilty towards those people. "I'm actually very careful, especially when it comes to money and things like that." Ter Schure said she spent an hour and a half warning people about the link that had been sent from her account. Afterwards her account was blocked by WhatsApp, probably as a precaution. "I can't get into WhatsApp at all anymore. I can't even get into the school app group." Not feeling guilty At the Fraudehelpdesk they recognise the trick. In recent days, dozens of reports came in. "We can't say exactly what it's related to," says a spokesperson. "But that the many data leaks make it easier for fraudsters to do this is certain." She calls the method "terribly deceptive". "People want to support a ballet dancer out of good intentions. Nobody does it on purpose. The fraudster is the one behind it." The Fraudehelpdesk urges people to be careful with these kinds of messages. "We all need to be very alert to the messages we receive. Pause and take the time to read it properly and think about it." Campaign That message is also central to a government campaign that starts today. Under the slogan 'Don't let yourself be tricked', the government urges people in the Netherlands to take three seconds before clicking on anything. "Doubt it? Then click away", advises the ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity>. According to Aad Lensen, project leader for digitised crime at the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, everyone runs the risk of being misled online. The moment and situation in which you receive the message play a decisive role, he says in a news item on the ministry's website. "It can really happen to anyone, especially at moments when you are in a hurry or distracted. So always give yourself three seconds before you click, respond or pay."

title: Another fatal accident at the Dordrecht ferry slipway, man (63) dies
lead: A 63-year-old man has died after an accident at the slipway to the ferry from Dordrecht to Werkendam. The two other occupants of the car, a woman (62) and a teenager, are still in hospital. The car went into the water at around 21.30 last evening. How exactly this could happen is still being investigated. According to regional broadcaster Rijnmond, the three occupants were pulled out of the water and resuscitated on the spot. The man died later in hospital. How the woman and the teenager are doing is unknown. According to the broadcaster, things have gone wrong more often in recent years at the spot where cars drive onto the ferry 'de Biesbosch'. In December 2024 a woman died after her car ended up in the water. After that fatal accident the municipality placed extra warning signs. The situation at the slipway to the ferry: The road runs into the slipway to the ferry. There is no barrier or gate. The relatives of the 63-year-old woman said in the media that visibility in the dark is poor at that spot. A friend of the woman said on behalf of the relatives that it is "a black hole in the evening". According to the municipality the current lighting meets the requirements. In 2020 and 2022, among other times, cars also ended up in the water at the slipway, but the drivers were able to get out unharmed then.

title: Bus of Qbuzz burns out in Hoogersmilde, passengers escape with a fright
lead: A Qbuzz bus caught fire in Hoogersmilde this morning. This happened on the N371, which runs through the Drenthe village. The bus on the Assen-Steenwijk line could be brought to a halt in time. All passengers and the driver were able to leave the vehicle in time. No one was injured. The vehicle, an articulated bus (also called a harmonica bus), has burned out. According to the fire brigade, it is a diesel bus. The cause of the fire is still unknown.

title: Rob Jetten and partner to become parents, 'a very special someone on the way'
lead: Rob Jetten is going to be a father. The prime minister and his partner, top hockey player Nicolás Keenan, announce the news via Instagram. 'There is a very special someone on the way. See you in 2027, little one,' they write. In the post the couple thanks their 'egg donor, our surrogate Lisa and their families'. 'Without you this would not have been possible.' The post is written in Dutch, Spanish and English. Keenan comes from Argentina, so he speaks Spanish. Jetten and Keenan have been engaged since 2024. When they will marry is not known. Contributing to a dream The child is expected in spring 2027. 'The surrogate and the baby are doing well, which is of course the most important thing for now,' says Jetten on the D66 website. He calls on people to respect the privacy of those involved. Surrogate Lisa also responds. 'I grew up warm and loving and now have a fantastic family of my own. With the unconditional support of our loved ones, surrogacy feels like a very special way to contribute and to help make the dream of our dear friends come true.'

title: Seawater bucket over Amalia at promotion to sergeant
lead: Princess Amalia was promoted from corporal to sergeant in the Royal Netherlands Navy this weekend. On a ship in the port of Den Helder she received her stripes from, among others, commander of the naval forces Vice Admiral Harold Liebregs. The 22-year-old crown princess was, as is customary, doused with a bucket of seawater, as shown in photos from the Ministry of Defence released by the <entity id="org:rijksvoorlichtingsdienst">Rijksvoorlichtingsdienst</entity> (RVD). The photos show only the moment just before the water was poured. The ceremony took place on board the Statsraad Lehmkuhl, a Norwegian three-masted ship from 1914 that the navy regularly uses as a training ship. In an RVD photo, Amalia can be seen saluting high up in the mast of the ship together with midshipmen (officers in training). Last year Amalia became the first female member of the Royal House to serve in the military when she began her training as a reservist at the Defensity College. She started in the lowest rank: seaman third class in the navy and private third class in the army and air force. In the part-time programme, students can gain work experience with the armed forces for up to three years and receive defence training. Amalia is combining it with her bachelor's in Dutch law at the University of Amsterdam. After completing basic training at the beginning of this year, Amalia was already promoted to corporal. Before the summer holiday she worked for a few months with the air force. The bucket of seawater that Amalia received has a long tradition in the navy as a rite of passage. The dousing stems from the practice of aging brand-new rank stripes as quickly as possible, to project more experience as an officer. At her promotion in January a similar ritual was performed and she was doused with beer over her epaulettes. That Amalia is now a sergeant does not mean her work changes much. At the moment she performs staff work, like all working students. Meanwhile she receives military training to gain good knowledge of the defence organisation. Ultimately, students of the Defensity College are meant to come out as lieutenants, the lowest officer rank. Lieutenants can lead a command of thirty people, but also perform other staff duties or specialist functions. Minister Yesilgöz of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-defensie">Defensie</entity> calls it "a beautiful milestone" for the princess. "Good to see how she is committing herself and developing within our armed forces. Respect to everyone who commits to our safety."

title: Countries promised to better protect their nature, but implementation is faltering
lead: To conserve nature, 30 percent of all land and sea on Earth must be protected area by 2030. Countries agreed to that four years ago in the Canadian city of Montreal. How is that promise going now? Over the next two weeks, countries are taking stock during a so-called biodiversity summit in the Armenian capital Yerevan. Minister <entity id="person:jaimi-van-essen">Jaimi van Essen</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-landbouw-visserij-voedselzekerheid-en-natuur">Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur</entity> is also attending. Biological diversity, or biodiversity for short, is a broad term. From primeval forests and elephants to the butterflies in your garden and the moss between the paving stones: it is all part of biodiversity. This concerns not only species of animals, plants, fungi and other life, but also the marshes, forests and other areas in which they live. Variation in the genetic material of species also falls under biodiversity. Pollination and coastal protection. Many people find nature worth protecting. But even if you don't, there are good reasons for nature conservation, says Christine Wortmann, who is going to the summit on behalf of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WNF). "Economic stability and food security are the strongest arguments." For example, wild bees help pollinate crops, and nature contributes to soil fertility. Nature areas also provide certain 'services' to people. For example, mangrove forests help protect the coast against flooding. In the Netherlands, for example, the so-called salt marshes help with this. 23 agreements. Worldwide, nature has declined over recent decades. That is why four years ago the countries made 23 agreements to protect a large part of the Earth and restore damaged nature. Many of those agreements are meant to support the fight against nature loss. For example, countries promised to phase out subsidies that harm nature and instead spend more money on protection. They also want, for instance, to create more green space in cities and make nature areas resilient to climate change. Not on track. This is not the first time countries have made agreements, but implementation proves stubborn. Once again the world is off track for most targets, as shown by a United Nations report published in July that the countries are discussing in Yerevan. Only one target was marked green: attention to the impact of climate change on nature. Correspondent Nina Jurna saw in 2024 how the Pantanal wetland is threatened: Otherwise, the verdict is mixed. "We are still reasonably satisfied with the progress on protecting 30 percent of the land and sea," says Wortmann of the WNF. She is less satisfied with the supporting measures. "Think of changing consumption patterns and raising money for nature protection." "The biggest problem is finding money to reach the targets," says Liesje Mommer, professor of underground ecology at Wageningen University, also speaking to the NOS Radio 1 Journaal. "It has been agreed that we need 200 billion euros a year to protect nature and biodiversity, but we are not yet halfway there." Phasing out subsidies. Talking about phasing out subsidies that destroy nature is also an important goal of the summit, Mommer says. The Netherlands published in May an overview of financial arrangements that affect biodiversity. Agriculture minister Van Essen wrote to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Kamer</entity> that <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> is working on "next steps" to do something with this report. For the negotiations, the Netherlands is cooperating with the European Union. Wortmann expects the EU to work to meet the agreements made in 2022 by 2030. In the negotiations this often causes tension with emerging countries, where most of the world's biodiversity is found. They feel they should receive more financial support to protect their rainforest and other nature. That should come from countries that have already become rich and have less nature to spare. The gathering in Yerevan is the seventeenth biodiversity summit. As early as 1992, nearly all countries in the world agreed in Rio de Janeiro to protect their nature. At the same time they also concluded the better-known climate treaty. The United States has not participated from the start, as one of the few UN members.

title: De Dag podcast: how the Bolsonaro dynasty is conquering Brazil
lead: Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, has a good chance of becoming president in the elections in Brazil this coming weekend. One of the first things he will then do is pardon his father, who was sentenced to 27 years in prison for an attempted coup. You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Like it? Don't forget to subscribe. Besides Flávio Bolsonaro, other Bolsonaros are also pushing into powerful positions, correspondent Nina Jurna tells in this podcast. How is it that Brazil, despite all the events, has embraced this family so massively? Reactions? Email dedag@nos.nl. Presentation and editing: Elisabeth Steinz. Editorial team: IJsbrand Terpstra. Final editor: Judith van de Hulsbeek

title: Again hundreds of thousands of households without power after Russian attacks on Kyiv
lead: Russia carried out missile and drone attacks overnight on power plants in Kyiv and surrounding regions. As a result, at least 550,000 households were left without power. Ukraine was also reportedly again not warned in advance of the missile attacks by Western intelligence services. Ukraine receives these warnings so it can alert citizens in time to an attack. Without those warnings, the country does not know when Russia will carry out an attack. Last week Zelensky already expressed his disappointment about not receiving intelligence earlier on Russian army actions. According to him, the American government is behind it. Russia reportedly launched sixteen ballistic missiles and two hundred drones overnight, spread over three waves of attacks. Besides power plants, a school, a metro station, a medical centre and shops were also hit. Zelensky writes this in a statement on X. The three waves of attacks took place around 23.00 last night, 03.00 this night and 07.00 this morning. According to journalists from The Kyiv Independent, during the first attack the air raid alarm only sounded when the missiles were already hitting. At least one person died and eight others were injured. According to Zelensky, Ukraine has welcomed every attempt to end the war or a ceasefire in a dignified way. Only Russia's response was always the same: new missile and drone attacks. Zelensky also accuses the United States of deliberately delaying Patriot deliveries to Ukraine. A Patriot is an air defence missile used, among other things, to shoot down ballistic missiles. Ukraine urgently needs these to defend itself against Russian missiles. Due to the slow deliveries, Ukraine's stock of air defence missiles has dropped to a critical level. Under the presidency of former president Joe Biden, Ukraine still received about 48 Patriot missiles per month; now under Trump it is only twelve. Uncertainty about intelligence The American Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied earlier today that the United States has stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. In doing so he contradicted Zelensky. During a visit to Uzbekistan, Rubio said that "Zelensky must focus on ending the war" and that "there has never been an interruption of intelligence". It is unclear exactly how things stand with the information supply. What is clear is that US pressure on Ukraine is increasing. During attacks last week, Ukraine also reportedly did not receive a warning about Russian missiles. In addition, last week there were problems with the Starlink satellite network. Ukraine is heavily dependent on that network. Problems with it limit the country's capabilities, including in attacks on Russia. In this special you can read how Starlink works and how indispensable the system is for Ukraine:

title: Dozens dead in Houthi attack on military base in Yemen
lead: The Houthis in Yemen have fired three ballistic missiles at a military camp of the Yemeni government. At least 53 people were killed, the local authorities of the southern province of Shabwa report. Also, 200 trainee soldiers were injured. The attack was on the al-Alam camp in the southern province of Shabwa. The provincial administration there says the death toll is preliminary and may still rise. The same applies to the number of injured. Earlier reports still assumed around twenty fatalities. The authorities speak of a "bloody and treacherous attack aimed at recruits in the training phase."
